Give every instance of an HA pair a persistent volume for its data directory (`--storage.path`). Without one, a
restarted instance loses its silences and its notification log: it can notify silenced alerts and send partial
Snapshots until the other instance catches it up.

## Token rotation

An Integration may hold several tokens. To rotate one without losing a webhook:

1. Create a second token and paste its snippet (or only the new `credentials`) into the Alertmanager configuration.
2. Reload Alertmanager and check that the token list shows a recent use of the new token.
3. Revoke the old token. It is refused from the next request.

A request with a revoked token is refused with `401` and counted under the Integration in
`muster_ingest_requests_total{outcome="unauthorized"}`, so the chart rule `MusterIngestRejected` shows an Alertmanager
that still uses an old token.

## Behind a reverse proxy

Muster serves ingestion on its own listener, `MUSTER_LISTEN_INGEST` (`:8081` by default), apart from the UI and API on
`MUSTER_LISTEN_APP`. Set `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` to the address Alertmanager uses; it defaults to `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL`, and
the snippets are built from it.

With separate listeners, route `/api/v1/ingest` and `/api/v1/heartbeat` (with everything below them) to the ingest
port. A reverse proxy that serves both on one host name, for example, sends these two paths to `:8081` and everything
else to `:8080`. Keep the proxy's body size limit at **16 MB** or more: Muster accepts bodies up to `ingest.body_limit`
(16 MB) and answers `413` above it. Do not let the proxy log request paths with the token, or prefer the
`Authorization` header, which proxies do not log by default.

With one listener for both (`MUSTER_LISTEN_INGEST` equal to `MUSTER_LISTEN_APP`), the same port serves ingestion and
the API.

## What Muster answers

| Answer | When | Alertmanager |
|---|---|---|
| `202` | The body was stored, whatever it holds | done |
| `401` | No token, an unknown or revoked token, a token of a deleted Integration, or an API token | does not retry |
| `413` | The body is larger than 16 MB | does not retry |
| `500` | The body could not be written | retries |

Muster never answers `400`: a body that is not JSON, or not an Alertmanager payload, is stored and fails later in
processing, where the Stored Snapshot shows the error.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md -->
# Connect Grafana

Grafana Alerting reaches Muster in one of two ways: directly, from Grafana's built-in Alertmanager through a webhook
contact point, or through an external Alertmanager that Grafana forwards its alerts to. Both carry Grafana-managed
alert rules.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  rules["Grafana alert rules"] --> builtin["Grafana's built-in Alertmanager"]
  builtin -- "Snapshots, webhook contact point" --> direct["Muster Integration for Grafana"]
  rules -. "alerts" .-> am["External Alertmanager"]
  prom["Prometheus rules"] -- "alerts" --> am
  am -- "Snapshots" --> shared["Muster Integration for the Alertmanager"]
```

- **Directly** needs nothing between Grafana and Muster. Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends Alertmanager's webhook
  format with a few fields of its own, and Muster reads each notification as a **Snapshot**, as from any Alertmanager.
- **Through an external Alertmanager** suits you when you already run an Alertmanager for Prometheus rules and want one
  Integration in Muster for both.

In the examples, `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is `https://ingest.muster.example.org`. Muster was tested with Grafana OSS 13.2.4,
as a single instance and as an HA pair.

## Connect Grafana directly

The steps, in this order: create an Integration and its token in Muster, create a webhook contact point in Grafana, and
send the alerts to it with a notification policy.

### One Integration per Grafana cluster and organization

Create one **Integration** for each Grafana cluster, and for each Grafana organization in it, that sends to Muster.

- An HA pair — two or more Grafana replicas that share a database and gossip with each other — is **one** cluster and
  gets **one** Integration. See [HA pairs](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#ha-pairs).
- Each Grafana organization gets an Integration of its own. The `groupKey` of a Snapshot names the notification policy
  and the group, not the organization, so two organizations with the same notification policies send the same
  `groupKey`s, and one Integration would take their Snapshots for one Alertmanager group.
- Give the Integration [Static labels](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#static-labels) for what the rules do not say, such as
  `cluster=prod-eu`.

### Create the Integration and a token

In **Integrations**, create the Integration, then **Create token**. Muster shows the token **once**, with a snippet for
Alertmanager; Grafana needs only the token (`mstr_int_…`), the `credentials` of that snippet. Copy it before you close
the dialog.

### Create a webhook contact point

In Grafana, open **Alerting** → **Contact points** → **Add contact point** and choose the integration **Webhook**:

1. **URL**: the Integration's ingest URL, `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` followed by `/api/v1/ingest`:
   `https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/ingest`.
2. **HTTP Method**: `POST`.
3. **Authorization header**: the scheme `Bearer`, and the Integration token as its credentials.
4. **Max alerts**: `0`, the default, which sends every alert of the group. Muster treats each Snapshot as the whole
   Alertmanager group; see [Limits](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#limits).
5. **Disable resolved message**: off, the default. Resolves close Alerts in Muster at once.
6. No custom payload: Muster reads the payload that Grafana sends by default, and a custom one replaces it.

Check these names against the version of Grafana that you run, because the places of the settings in the interface
change between versions. The same contact point in a provisioning file, together with the notification policy of the
next step:

```yaml
apiVersion: 1

contactPoints:
  - orgId: 1
    name: muster
    receivers:
      - uid: muster
        type: webhook
        disableResolveMessage: false
        settings:
          url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/ingest
          httpMethod: POST
          authorization_scheme: Bearer
          authorization_credentials: ${MUSTER_TOKEN}

policies:
  - orgId: 1
    receiver: muster
    group_by: [grafana_folder, alertname]
    repeat_interval: 10m
```

Grafana replaces `${MUSTER_TOKEN}` with the variable of its environment when it reads the file, so the token stays out
of the file. The file leaves out Max alerts (`maxAlerts`), so it is 0. Grafana does not let you edit resources
provisioned from files in its interface, this contact point and the notification policy tree included: change the
file, then restart Grafana or reload the provisioned files through its Admin API.

### Send the alerts with a notification policy

In **Alerting** → **Notification policies**, send the alerts to the contact point:

- Keep Grafana's default grouping, `group_by: [grafana_folder, alertname]`, and let Muster make Alert Groups with its
  [Routes and Group keys](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md). See
  [Do not merge rules into one group](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#do-not-merge-rules-into-one-group).
- Set `repeat_interval` between **5 and 15 minutes** (10 minutes in the example). See
  [Repeat intervals](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#repeat-intervals).
- The example makes Muster the contact point of the default policy, which takes every alert. A provisioned `policies`
  entry is the whole notification policy tree of the organization and replaces the one set in the user interface. If
  Grafana also notifies other contact points, add Muster instead as the first nested policy, without matchers, with
  `continue: true` and its own `repeat_interval`, and keep a last nested policy for your default contact point, as for
  the [Alertmanager route](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#create-a-token-and-paste-the-snippet).
- Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends the notifications, so keep it receiving Grafana-managed alerts, the default in
  **Alerting** → **Settings**.

On its first start, Grafana applies provisioned policies within about a minute. Grafana sends the first Snapshot when
an alert fires; the Integration page then shows the time of the last Snapshot and the Stored Snapshots as received.

### Repeat intervals

Repeats are how Muster learns when an alert is **Gone** or **Stale**, as with Alertmanager; see
[Repeat intervals](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#repeat-intervals). Grafana sends no `notification_reason`, so Muster recognises a
repeat as a Snapshot identical to the one before it and learns the interval from those.

Grafana sends a repeat on the first `group_interval` tick after `repeat_interval` has elapsed. With 10 minutes and
Grafana's default `group_interval` of 5 minutes, Muster learns an interval of about 15 minutes; with Grafana's default
`repeat_interval` of 4 hours, an Alert of a silent group would go Stale only after more than 12 hours. Control the noise
in Muster, not with a long interval: Muster sends one message per Alert Group and edits it, so a repeat changes nothing
that people see.

### Do not merge rules into one group

Keep each Grafana notification group to the alerts of one rule, as the default grouping by `grafana_folder` and
`alertname` does, and do not group many rules together, for example by a label that they share.

After a restart, Grafana knows the alerts of a rule again only once it has evaluated the rule. A group of rules with
different evaluation intervals then sends Snapshots without the slower rules' alerts until their first evaluation: in
a test, the alert of a rule evaluated every 8 minutes was missing from its group's Snapshots for about 7 minutes. Muster
can take such an alert for Gone, and its return for a new firing, which is Loud. Grafana has no setting like
Alertmanager's [start delay](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#start-delay). The alerts of one rule all return with its first evaluation,
and Muster's Routes put them into Alert Groups as they would any other alerts.

### Simplified routing

A contact point chosen in the rule itself (simplified routing) puts the label `__grafana_route_settings_hash__`, a hash
of the rule's notification settings, into the route path of the `groupKey`. Editing those settings starts a new
`groupKey`, and the old one falls silent, as when the matchers of an Alertmanager route change: an Alert that the new
`groupKey` lists stays firing, and one that only the old `groupKey` listed resolves only by going Stale, which needs a
live [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#heartbeat). Notification policies avoid this.

### What Grafana sends

- **Every end of an alert is an explicit resolve**: a value back under the threshold, a series that is missing for two
  evaluations, a paused rule and a deleted rule. Muster resolves the Alert at once, with the reason `resolved`. Grafana
  gives the resolve the annotation `grafana_state_reason` (`MissingSeries`, `Paused` or `RuleDeleted`); Muster takes
  annotations from firing alerts only, so that reason shows in the Stored Snapshot, not on the Alert.
- **NoData and Error are alerts of their own.** A rule whose query returns no data, with the no-data state No Data,
  resolves its alert and fires an alert `DatasourceNoData` in a group of its own, with the label `rulename` (the rule's
  title), `datasource_uid` and `ref_id` beside the rule's labels. When data returns, the rule's alert fires again as a
  new firing and `DatasourceNoData` resolves. The error state Error gives an alert `DatasourceError` with the label
  `rulename` the same way, as Grafana documents it; it has not been tested with Muster. A Route can match both by
  `alertname`.
- **Links.** The **Source** link of an Alert Group opens the rule's page in Grafana, the alert's `generatorURL`:
  `<root_url>/alerting/grafana/<rule uid>/view?orgId=1`. Set Grafana's `root_url` to the address people open. The
  built-in Link rule Explore builds its link from the Prometheus query of a `generatorURL`, which Grafana's does not
  have, so it makes no link for Grafana's alerts.

### HA pairs

An HA pair needs nothing more than its one Integration and one contact point. Normally one replica sends; when both do,
Muster folds their copies together within the Integration's duplicate window.

The replicas evaluate the rules each on its own, so their copies of one alert can carry different `startsAt`. Muster
takes the resolve of either replica: a resolve whose firing overlaps the current one resolves it (see
[Resolved](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md#resolved)). Such copies can also make Muster record a Quiet Continuation
for an Alert once. Grafana's `ha_single_node_evaluation`, which makes one replica evaluate the rules for both, has not
been tested with Muster.

### Heartbeat

The [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md) page's setup is for Alertmanager. The same idea in Grafana — an always-firing rule with a
notification policy of its own, a `repeat_interval` of about one minute, and a second webhook contact point at the
Integration's Heartbeat URL, `https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat`, with resolved messages disabled —
**has not been verified with Grafana**.

Without a Heartbeat, Muster never resolves an Alert as Stale: an Alert whose Grafana group stops sending altogether
stays firing in Muster. Gone still works. A cron job that requests the Heartbeat URL keeps the Heartbeat live too, but
it proves only the network: when Grafana itself stops, its groups fall silent and their Alerts go Stale.

### Limits

- **Truncation.** With Max alerts above 0, a Snapshot lists only part of its group. Muster keeps the unlisted Alerts
  alive and raises the Internal alert `MusterSnapshotTruncated`
  ([runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterSnapshotTruncated.md)). Grafana computes the status of a Snapshot from the
  alerts it lists, so a truncated Snapshot can say `resolved` while alerts it left out still fire; Muster recognises a
  Snapshot from Grafana by its top-level `orgId`, and a truncated `status: resolved` from Grafana resolves only the
  Alerts it lists as resolved. When a whole group resolves, its last Snapshot too lists only the first alerts, and
  Grafana sends nothing more for the group until one of its alerts fires again: the Alerts it left out stay firing in
  Muster until they go Stale, which needs a live [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#heartbeat). Set Max alerts to 0; for the Alerts already
  left firing, see the [runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterSnapshotTruncated.md#fix).
- **The Integration page speaks of Alertmanager**, the part that Grafana's built-in one plays. Its Alertmanager routes
  are Grafana's notification policies; its warning about a long repeat interval shows an Alertmanager route, where for
  Grafana you set the `repeat_interval` of the policy; its truncation warning names `max_alerts`, which is Max alerts
  in Grafana.
- [What Muster answers](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#what-muster-answers), [Token rotation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#token-rotation) and
  [Behind a reverse proxy](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy) apply to Grafana as they are.
- **Not tested with Muster**: Grafana's retries of a webhook after an error or a timeout; Grafana's silences and mute
  timings; several Grafana organizations on one Integration; a custom payload; HMAC signing (Muster checks the
  Integration token only); `ha_single_node_evaluation`; `DatasourceError`; the Heartbeat through Grafana.

## Connect Grafana through an external Alertmanager

Grafana-managed alert rules can also reach Muster the same way as Prometheus rules do: Grafana forwards its alerts to
an external Alertmanager, and that Alertmanager has the Muster receiver from [Connect Alertmanager](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md).
One Alertmanager can serve Grafana and Prometheus together, with one Integration in Muster for the whole Alertmanager
cluster.

Prefer this way when you already run an Alertmanager for Prometheus rules and want one Integration for both: the
Heartbeat route of the [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md) page then watches the path of Grafana's alerts too.

### Send Grafana's alerts to the Alertmanager

In Grafana, two settings are needed, and both must be on.

1. Add the Alertmanager as a data source: **Connections** → **Data sources** → **Alertmanager**. Set the
   **Alertmanager Implementation** (Prometheus, for a plain Alertmanager) and the **HTTP URL**, and turn on **Receive
   Grafana Alerts**.
2. In **Alerting** → **Settings** (called Administration in some versions), enable that Alertmanager so that it shows
   that it receives Grafana-managed alerts.

From then on Grafana forwards all its Grafana-managed alerts to the Alertmanager. The same data source in a
provisioning file, which covers step 1 only; step 2 is still done in **Alerting** → **Settings**:

```yaml
apiVersion: 1

datasources:
  - name: Alertmanager
    type: alertmanager
    url: http://alertmanager.monitoring.svc:9093
    access: proxy
    jsonData:
      implementation: prometheus
      handleGrafanaManagedAlerts: true
```

The option in the user interface is **Receive Grafana Alerts**; its `jsonData` name is `handleGrafanaManagedAlerts`. The
names above are those of the Grafana documentation of the Alertmanager data source; check the version of Grafana that
you run, because the places of the settings in the interface change between versions.

Then follow [Connect Alertmanager](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md): create an Integration for the Alertmanager, paste the receiver and
the route into its configuration, and keep the catch-all child route last.

## Labels

Grafana adds two labels of its own to every Grafana-managed alert: `alertname`, the name of the alert rule, and
`grafana_folder`, the title of the folder that holds the rule. Labels that you set on the rule, such as `severity` or
`team`, come with them. Route and Group key on these labels in Muster as on any others:

- Set `severity` on your rules: it is part of the default Group key, and Routes can match it.
- `alertname` is also part of the default Group key, so rules of different names make different Alert Groups.
- Grafana rules have no `cluster` label of their own: add it to the Integration as a
  [Static label](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#static-labels). Through an Alertmanager shared with Prometheus, you can instead give
  Grafana's alerts an Integration of their own.
- A rule on a query that returns one series per pod or instance makes one alert per series, with those labels. Keep
  [Instance labels out of informational alerts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#instance-labels-in-informational-alerts); a Grafana
  rule can reduce the series to one with an aggregation.
- Directly from Grafana, an Alert's fingerprint is the one in the body, which also covers the rule's hidden uid, so two
  rules with the same labels make two Alerts.

Muster shows the labels of each alert on the page of its Alert Group. If a label you expected is missing, open the
Stored Snapshot on the Integration page, which shows the request as Grafana or the Alertmanager sent it.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md -->
# Heartbeat

A **Heartbeat** proves, for one Integration, that the path from your cluster to Muster works: Prometheus evaluates
rules, Alertmanager sends notifications, and the network carries them to Muster. Alertmanager sends Muster a signal
about once a minute; when the signals stop, Muster calls people. It is part of the recommended setup of every
Integration.

In the examples, `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is `https://ingest.muster.example.org`.

## Why it matters

Without a Heartbeat, a silent Alertmanager looks exactly like a healthy cluster with nothing to report. With one:

- Muster notices when Alertmanager goes quiet. After the Heartbeat timeout without a signal, the Integration is
  **Heartbeat lost** and Muster raises the Internal alert `MusterHeartbeatLost` (severity `critical`). Its labels are
  `integration` (the Integration's id), `integration_name` and the Integration's Static labels, so a Route can send it
  to the team of that cluster.
- Muster can resolve alerts as **Stale**. An Alertmanager group that is silenced, inhibited or muted as a whole sends
  nothing at all, not even its resolves, so Muster resolves its alerts once it has not seen them for three learned
  repeat intervals. It does that only while it knows that it would have heard from Alertmanager: while the Heartbeat is
  live. An Integration without a Heartbeat never resolves alerts as Stale.

## Turn it on

On the Integration page, turn the Heartbeat on. The timeout is 5 minutes by default (`integration.heartbeat_timeout`);
keep it a few times the interval at which Alertmanager signals. The Heartbeat then **waits for the first signal**:
nothing is raised and nothing goes Stale until it arrives, however long that takes. The first signal makes it
**live**.

While the Heartbeat is off, Muster answers a signal with `204` and records nothing, so turning it on later always
starts from waiting. Turning it off resolves an open `MusterHeartbeatLost`.

## The Heartbeat URL

Each Integration has its Heartbeat URL on the ingest listener:

```text
https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat
```

It accepts `GET` and `POST` with one of the Integration's tokens as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, or appended to the
path as `/api/v1/heartbeat/<token>`, and answers `204`. The body is ignored. A missing, wrong or revoked token, or an
API token, is refused with `401`. Muster's logs name only the route, never a path with a token.

## The snippet

With the Heartbeat on, **Create token** also shows a Heartbeat snippet, **once**, with the token in it. It has three
parts.

An alert that always fires, as a Prometheus rule:

```yaml
groups:
  - name: muster-heartbeat
    rules:
      - alert: MusterHeartbeat
        expr: vector(1)
```

kube-prometheus-stack already has such an alert, **`Watchdog`**. With it, skip the rule and match
`alertname="Watchdog"` in the route instead.

A child route for it, first under the top-level route:

```yaml
route:
  routes:
    - receiver: muster-heartbeat-prod-eu
      matchers: ['alertname="MusterHeartbeat"']
      continue: true
      group_wait: 0s
      group_interval: 1m
      repeat_interval: 1m
```

`repeat_interval: 1m` (`snippet.heartbeat_repeat_interval`) makes Alertmanager send the always-firing alert about once
a minute, and `continue: true` passes it on to your other routes, such as a dead man's switch.

A receiver that sends it to the Heartbeat URL, without resolves:

```yaml
receivers:
  - name: muster-heartbeat-prod-eu
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat
        send_resolved: false
        http_config:
          authorization:
            type: Bearer
            credentials: mstr_int_…
```

Reload Alertmanager. Within a minute or two the Integration's Heartbeat becomes live.

## A cron job also works, but proves less

Any client that requests the Heartbeat URL regularly keeps the Heartbeat live, for example a cron job:

```sh
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/heartbeat
```

It proves only that the network from that host to Muster works. The Alertmanager route proves much more: that
Prometheus evaluates rules, that Alertmanager routes and sends notifications, and that they reach Muster, which is
exactly the path your alerts take. Prefer it.

## When the Heartbeat is lost

No signal within the timeout makes the Integration **Heartbeat lost**:

- Muster raises `MusterHeartbeatLost` as a firing Alert of the built-in "Muster" Integration, and the Integration shows
  since when Muster has had no contact: the time of the last signal.
- **Stale resolution pauses.** The time without a live Heartbeat, from the last signal before the loss until the
  signal returns, does not count towards an alert's time to go Stale, so a broken path never resolves alerts that may
  still fire.
- The chart's rule `MusterHeartbeatLost` on `muster_heartbeat_lost` is the backup when Muster itself cannot deliver.

The next signal makes the Heartbeat live again and resolves `MusterHeartbeatLost`. Deleting the Integration resolves it
too.

After Muster itself was down, the timeout counts from the moment the Leader started leading again, so that Muster's own
outage does not make every Integration Heartbeat lost. A downtime longer than the timeout does not count towards
staleness either; a shorter one does, which is at most the timeout against at least three repeat intervals.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/index.md -->
# Messengers

Muster delivers Alert Groups to **Destinations**. A Destination is a place where Alert Groups arrive: a channel of a
messenger, or an outgoing webhook. There are five types:

- **Mattermost**, through a bot account on your Mattermost server;
- **Slack**, through the bot of a Slack app, to a channel the bot is a member of;
- **Telegram**, through a bot, to a channel with comments;
- **Bridge**, for any other messenger: a small service that you or someone else writes speaks the Bridge protocol with
  Muster and talks to the messenger;
- **Outgoing webhook**, which sends the lifecycle events of Alert Groups, or requests you build from templates, to any HTTP
  endpoint.

A **Connection** holds the credentials Muster uses to reach one messenger: a bot on a Mattermost server, the bot of a
Slack app, a Telegram bot, or a Bridge. Many Destinations can share a Connection. An outgoing webhook has no Connection;
the Destination carries its own address, Secrets and proxy.

To start, create the Connection, check it, create a Destination for a channel, and add the Destination to a Route. A Route
decides which Alert Groups reach which Destinations; see [Routes and Group keys](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md).

## What each Destination type can do

Every entry is true for this release. An entry that depends on the bridge says "if the bridge declares it": a Bridge
offers only what its `info` announces, and Muster adapts to the rest. [Write a bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/write-a-bridge.md) lists the
features.

Needs a Connection
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — yes
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — no

One message per Alert Group, kept up to date
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — yes
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no: one request per event
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, through your requests

Edits of the Root message
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes, no window known
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — yes, until the bridge's edit window
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, through the `update` request

Buttons
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes, with the Snooze menu
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — if the bridge declares `buttons`
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — no

Without buttons
:   - Mattermost — the web UI and the API
    - Slack — the web UI and the API
    - Telegram — the web UI and the API
    - Bridge — [Text commands](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#text-commands) in the Thread if the bridge declares
      `thread_messages`; otherwise the web UI and the API
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — the web UI and the API
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — the web UI and the API

Thread
:   - Mattermost — replies under the Root message
    - Slack — replies under the Root message
    - Telegram — the comments of the Root message, in the channel's discussion group
    - Bridge — replies under the Root message
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no: each event is separate
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — optional `reply_in_thread`, with an optional `open_thread`

Loud
:   - Mattermost — a new post with Mentions
    - Slack — a new message with Mentions
    - Telegram — a new message
    - Bridge — a new message that the bridge posts with `notify`
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — `notify` is true
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — `.Notify` is true

Quiet
:   - Mattermost — an edit, or a post without a Mention
    - Slack — an edit, or a message without a Mention
    - Telegram — an edit, or a message sent with `disable_notification`
    - Bridge — an edit, or a message without a notification if the bridge declares `quiet_messages`
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — `notify` is false
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — `.Notify` is false

Mentions
:   - Mattermost — nobody, `@channel` `@all` `@here`, users, Mattermost groups
    - Slack — nobody, `@channel` `@here`, users
    - Telegram — nobody, users
    - Bridge — nobody, users
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — nobody, everyone, users, groups, as data
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — the same, as data

Account links
:   - Mattermost — yes: a code the bot sends by direct message
    - Slack — yes: a code the bot sends by direct message
    - Telegram — yes: a link that opens the bot
    - Bridge — yes: a token sent to the bot, and a code if the bridge can find people and send direct messages
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — not needed: no one presses anything
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — not needed

Rate limits
:   - Mattermost — Connection 5 requests/s; Destination the same by default
    - Slack — Connection 50 requests/min; Destination 30 requests/min, sends and edits together
    - Telegram — Connection 15 messages/s; Destination 10 requests/min, sends and edits together
    - Bridge — Connection 10 requests/s, Destination 30 requests/min, or half of what the bridge's info declares
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — Destination 5 requests/s
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — Destination 5 requests/s

Edit window
:   - Mattermost — none by default; the server setting `PostEditTimeLimit` is unlimited, so keep it
    - Slack — none known for a bot's messages
    - Telegram — none for the bot's own messages
    - Bridge — the bridge declares it, or none; Muster publishes a new Root message past it
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — not applicable
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — the chat's own; Muster does not know it

Storms
:   - Mattermost — one Storm summary per Route
    - Slack — one Storm summary per Route
    - Telegram — one Storm summary per Route
    - Bridge — one Storm summary per Route
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — every event is sent, no summary
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — one Storm summary

Proxy
:   - Mattermost — on the Connection
    - Slack — on the Connection
    - Telegram — on the Connection
    - Bridge — on the Connection
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — on the Destination
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — on the Destination

Destination check
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes, `conversations.info`
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — yes, `checkChannel`, which posts nothing
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — no
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — no

Test message and preview
:   - Mattermost — yes
    - Slack — yes, the test message cannot press its own button
    - Telegram — yes
    - Bridge — yes
    - Outgoing webhook, events mode — yes, sends the event `test`
    - Outgoing webhook, template mode — yes, sends the `create` request

Notes on the entries:

- **Rate limits.** These are the defaults of the limiters, and you can change them. Mattermost's own rate limit is off
  by default; when an administrator turns it on, it allows 10 requests per second per client address, so keep the
  limiters of all Connections to one server below that together. Slack limits each method per app and workspace, and
  about one message per second per channel; its Connection limiter is 50 requests a minute and its Destination limiter
  30. A Telegram chat takes about 20 messages and edits per minute, which is why its Destination limiter is half of
  that. A bridge says its own limits in its info, and its `rate_limited` answers always win. A `429` from a messenger
  holds the Destinations that share it, for as long as it asks.
- **Slack and Quiet.** Slack cannot send a message without a notification, so Quiet means "without a Mention"; an edit
  carries no Mention. See [Connect Slack](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md#who-gets-notified).
- **Account links.** Pressing a button as a Muster user, and being Mentioned, need an Account link. See [Link your
  messenger accounts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md).
- **Loud and Quiet.** Edits never notify anybody, so every Loud change is a new message. See [Loud and
  Quiet](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md).
- **Edit windows.** See [Broken Destinations](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md#republishing-past-an-edit-window).
- **Destination check.** It asks the messenger whether the bot can still post, without posting. Muster runs it when you save
  a Destination, from **Check**, and as the probe of a [Broken Destination](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md) when nothing
  waits. An outgoing webhook has no Destination check, so a Broken one is probed by its next delivery.

## Pages

- [Connect Mattermost](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/mattermost.md): the bot account, the setting that lets the server call Muster for button presses,
  and who gets notified.
- [Connect Slack](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md): the app and its manifests for Socket Mode and for HTTP, the tokens, the bot in the
  channels, and who gets notified.
- [Connect Telegram](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram.md): the bot, a channel with comments, long polling or a webhook;
  [Telegram in restricted networks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md) for networks where it is blocked.
- [Connect a messenger through a bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/bridge.md), and [Write a bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/write-a-bridge.md) for a messenger Muster does not
  support.
- [Outgoing webhooks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/events.md): the [events mode](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/events.md), the [template
  mode](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/templates.md) and some [recipes](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/recipes.md).
- [Proxies](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/proxies.md): the proxy of each client, and what the outbound address policy checks.
- [Link your messenger accounts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md): how people tie their messenger accounts to their Muster user.
- [Request log](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/request-log.md): the recent requests Muster sent to a messenger, a bridge or an outgoing
  webhook, with secrets masked, for troubleshooting.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/mattermost.md -->
# Connect Mattermost

Muster posts to Mattermost through the REST API with a **bot account**: one post per Alert Group, the **Root
message**, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes, and replies in its **Thread** for what happens later. People
act on the Alert Group with the buttons of the post. Muster uses no incoming webhook and no plugin.

In the examples, `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` is `https://muster.example.org`, `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is
`https://ingest.muster.example.org` and the Mattermost server is `https://chat.example.org`.

## Create the bot account

1. In the System Console, under **Integrations → Bot Accounts**, turn on **Enable Bot Account Creation**.
2. In **Integrations → Bot Accounts**, add a bot, for example `muster`. Give it the role **Member**: Muster needs no
   system admin role and no **post:all** or **post:channels** permission, because it posts only to channels the bot
   is a member of. With the role Member, the answers to button presses show in the Thread of the Root message; see
   [Where answers to presses show](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/mattermost.md#where-answers-to-presses-show).
3. Copy the bot's access token. Mattermost shows it once.
4. Add the bot to the team, and to every channel a Destination posts to. A public channel is enough; a private channel
   works the same once the bot is a member.

The bot token works even when **Enable Personal Access Tokens** is off, its default.

In Muster, create a **Connection** of type Mattermost with the server's address and the bot token, then **Check** it:
the check reads the bot's own user with the token and shows the bot's name. Then create a **Destination** for each
channel; saving it checks that the bot is a member of the channel and refuses the Destination otherwise, naming the
failing check.

## Check before saving

**Check connection** also works in the form, before anything is saved: in the form of a new Connection, and on the
page of a saved one while the form holds changes. It checks the values in the form — the server URL, the proxy and the
bot token, if you typed one — and saves nothing: no bot name is recorded and the Audit log gets no entry.

- With the bot token typed in the form, the check reads the bot's own user at the server URL in the form, through the
  proxy in the form, and shows the bot's name.
- Without a token typed, the page of a saved Connection uses its stored token only when the server URL and the proxy
  are the saved ones: the stored token is sent only to the saved address, through the saved proxy. After a change of
  the server URL or of the proxy, the check makes only a dry probe: `GET <server>/api/v4/system/ping` without a token,
  which a Mattermost server answers to anyone with `200` and `"status":"OK"`. It tells a wrong address, a wrong path
  prefix (`404`) and a server that is not Mattermost apart, and the step **Token** asks you to type the bot token again
  to check the new address or proxy, or to save first. A new Connection without a token gets the dry probe alone too.

The check is `POST /api/v1/connections/checks`, which needs `connections:write`; with a Personal access token of an
Admin in `MUSTER_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"mattermost","server_url":"https://chat.example.org","bot_token":"the-bot-token"}'
```

Add `"connection_id":"CN…"` to check the changes of a saved Connection, whose stored token the rule above may use.

## Direct messages

Account links send a person a direct message from the bot: the bot opens the direct channel with the person's user id
and posts there. Make sure your server lets the bot open direct messages with the people who link their accounts — for
example, if **Enable users to open Direct Message channels with** is restricted to members of a team, add the bot to
the teams of those people.

## Let button presses reach Muster

A press on a button makes the Mattermost server call Muster at the Connection's callback address, which the Connection
page shows:

```text
https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/mattermost/CN…
```

When that address resolves to a private or otherwise reserved address — the usual case inside one network — the
Mattermost server refuses to call it unless the host is listed in **ServiceSettings.AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections**
(**Environment → Developer → Allow untrusted internal connections to** in the System Console). Add the host of
`MUSTER_INGEST_URL`, for example:

```json
"ServiceSettings": {
  "AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections": "ingest.muster.example.org"
}
```

Without it, a person who presses a button sees only a generic **Action integration error**; only the Mattermost server
log says why ("address forbidden … in a reserved range and not in AllowedUntrustedInternalConnections"). The test
message of a Destination presses its own button through the bot and tells you whether the press reached Muster.

Whatever the person who pressed must read — that the press was refused, that their Mattermost account is not linked
to Muster yet, or that the button could not be verified — arrives as a message only they can see. A press from an
account without an Account link changes nothing. A request that does not come from a button of a Muster post in one of
the Connection's channels gets no answer at all.

### Where answers to presses show

Muster first sends the answer as an ephemeral message, which shows in the channel, marked "(Only visible to you)".
Mattermost allows that only with the `create_post_ephemeral` permission, which by default only the system admin role
has. Without it, Mattermost refuses the ephemeral message, and Muster returns the same text in its answer to the press:
Mattermost then shows it from **System** in the **Thread** of the Root message. With collapsed reply threads,
Mattermost's default, it is not shown in the channel view; the person opens the Thread to read it. Either way the answer
is never lost.

**Check connection** tells you which applies: when the bot's roles do not grant `create_post_ephemeral`, the check
passes with a warning that answers will show in the Thread of the Root message, and `muster doctor` prints the
Connection as a `WARN` line. To show answers in the channel, give the bot that permission, for example the system admin
role. Otherwise keep the role Member and let people read the answers in the Thread.

## Rate limit

Mattermost's rate limit is off by default. When an admin turns it on (`RateLimitSettings.Enable`, which takes a server
restart), it allows 10 requests per second, with a burst of 100, **per client address**. All Connections of one Muster
installation to the same Mattermost server usually come from one address and share that bucket, so keep their limiters
together below it. The default limiter of a Connection is 5 requests per second. A `429` from Mattermost holds every
request of the Connection, to any of its Destinations, for the seconds of its `Retry-After`.

## Keep posts editable

Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group is open, which can be days. Keep
**ServiceSettings.PostEditTimeLimit** at `-1`, its default, so that posts can be edited at any age.

## Who gets notified

- **Edits notify nobody**, even an edit that adds a Mention. That is why every Loud event is a new post: a new Root
  message, or a reply in the Thread.
- **Thread replies notify the Thread's followers** by their own notification settings, and a Mention makes the person
  mentioned a follower of the Thread. "Quiet" therefore means "without a Mention", not "nobody notified".
- A Loud post carries its Mentions — `@channel`, `@here`, `@all`, a Mattermost group, or a person's `@username` through
  their Account link — in the post's text, never in the attachment, so that the notification shows what happened. A
  `{{ mention "channel" }}` in a Route's template shows in the attachment as text and, on a Loud post, adds its Mention
  to the post's text.
- Alert data never mention anyone: an `@` in a label or annotation is shown as text and notifies nobody. The footer of
  a Root message names a person by their username without `@`, which does not notify them either.

## Check from the command line

`muster doctor` prints one line per Mattermost Connection and per Mattermost Destination with the same checks, without
sending anything.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram.md -->
# Connect Telegram

Muster posts to a Telegram **channel** through the Bot API with a **bot**: one channel post per Alert Group, the
**Root message**, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes. Everything that happens later goes to the channel's
**discussion group**, the group that Telegram creates when comments are enabled on the channel. People act on the Alert
Group with the buttons under the post.

In the examples, `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is `https://ingest.muster.example.org` and the bot is `@muster_alerts_bot`.

## Create the bot

1. In Telegram, open [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) and send `/newbot`. Give the bot a name and a username, for
   example `@muster_alerts_bot`.
2. Copy the bot token that BotFather sends, such as `123456789:AA…`. Anyone with the token controls the bot; Muster
   stores it encrypted and never shows it again.
3. Leave the bot's privacy mode on, the default. Muster needs no other setting in BotFather.

In Muster, create a **Connection** of type Telegram with the bot token, then **Check** it. Its **Bot API base URL** is
`https://api.telegram.org` unless Telegram is blocked in your network; for a proxy or another address, see
[Telegram in restricted networks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md). The check runs in steps and shows the latency of
each and whether it went through the proxy:

1. a dry probe, `GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe` without your token, which only a Bot API answers with `401` and JSON — it
   tells a wrong address, a wrong path prefix, a proxy that refuses or a web server that is not a Bot API apart before
   your token goes anywhere;
2. `getMe` with your token, which names the bot;
3. `getWebhookInfo`, which says whether a webhook is set and how many updates wait.

## Check before saving

**Check connection** also works in the form, before anything is saved: in the form of a new Connection, and on the
page of a saved one while the form holds changes. It checks the values in the form — the Bot API base URL, the update
mode, the proxy and the bot token, if you typed one — and saves nothing: no bot name is recorded and the Audit log gets
no entry.

- With the bot token typed in the form, the check runs its three steps against the base URL in the form, through the
  proxy in the form, with that token.
- Without a token typed, the page of a saved Connection uses its stored token only when the base URL — a trailing `/`
  aside — and the proxy are the saved ones: the stored token is sent only to the saved address, through the saved
  proxy, since a proxy you have not saved would see it in the path of an `http` base URL. After a change of the base
  URL or of the proxy, the check makes only the dry probe there, `GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe` without your token, and
  `getMe` and `getWebhookInfo` ask you to type the bot token again to check the new address or proxy, or to save
  first. A new Connection without a token gets the dry probe alone too.

The check is `POST /api/v1/connections/checks`, which needs `connections:write`; with a Personal access token of an
Admin in `MUSTER_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl -X POST https://muster.example.org/api/v1/connections/checks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"type":"telegram","bot_api_base_url":"https://api.telegram.org","update_mode":"long_polling",
       "bot_token":"123456789:AA…"}'
```

Add `"connection_id":"CN…"` to check the changes of a saved Connection, whose stored token the rule above may use.

## Enable comments on the channel

A Telegram Destination is a channel **with comments**. Comments on a channel post live in the channel's discussion
group, and Muster writes everything about an Alert Group after its Root message there.

1. Create the channel, or open an existing one.
2. In the channel's settings, open **Discussion** and add a group, or let Telegram create one. This enables comments,
   and Telegram links the group to the channel.

You never enter the group in Muster: the Destination check finds it through the channel.

## Make the bot an admin of the channel and of the group

1. In the channel's settings, under **Administrators**, add the bot. Telegram adds a bot to a channel only as an admin:
   added as a subscriber, it stays outside the channel. Allow it to **post messages** and to **edit messages of
   others**; Muster needs both, because it edits its own posts as the Alert Group changes.
2. In the discussion group's settings, under **Administrators**, add the bot as well. An admin may always post in the
   group. The bot must be an admin, not a plain member: Telegram does not send a bot that is a plain member the copies
   of the channel's posts in the group, which the Threads of the Root messages hang under.

In Muster, create a **Destination** of type Telegram with the Connection and the channel only — its chat id, such as
`-1001234567890`, or `@username` for a public channel. Saving it runs the **Destination check**:

- `getChat` on the channel: it exists and is a channel, and it names its discussion group;
- `getChatMember` for the bot in the channel: an admin allowed to post and to edit messages;
- `getChatMember` for the bot in the discussion group: an admin there.

A Destination that fails the check is not saved, and the check says what to fix:

- "Comments are not enabled for this channel. Enable comments in the channel settings in Telegram; this creates its
  discussion group."
- "The bot is not an admin of the discussion group {group}. Make the bot an admin there, allowed to post messages."
- "The bot is not an admin of the channel.", "The bot may not post messages in the channel." or "The bot may not edit
  messages in the channel."

The Destination then shows the discussion group it found. Muster keeps sending to that channel and that group: when
comments are moved to another group later, or the `@username` to another channel, the check fails with "The channel or
its discussion group changed since the Destination was saved. Save the Destination again." until you save it. **Check** on the Destination page runs the same check at any
time, and `muster doctor` prints one line per Telegram Destination with its result. When Telegram refuses the bot later
— for example, someone removed its admin rights — the Destination becomes **Broken**; Muster runs the same check every
few minutes while nothing waits for the Destination, and ends the Broken state once the check passes again.

## Long polling or webhook

Muster receives the bot's updates — button presses and the messages of the discussion group — in one of two **update
modes**, set on the Connection:

- **Long polling**, the default. The Leader asks Telegram for updates with `getUpdates`. Muster needs no public address:
  it only calls out to Telegram. Only one process may poll a bot: when a second one starts — another
  Muster installation with the same token, or a test script — Telegram ends one of the polls with `409 Conflict`, and
  the two then take turns. Muster backs off and logs `telegram_poll_conflict`; the Destination does not become Broken.
  Give each installation its own bot.
- **Webhook**. Telegram posts each update to Muster at
  `https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/telegram/CN…`, under `MUSTER_INGEST_URL`, with a secret token
  header that Muster checks. Saving the Connection in this mode calls `setWebhook`; leaving the mode, or deleting the
  Connection, calls `deleteWebhook`. Use the webhook mode when Telegram can reach `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` over HTTPS.

Where Telegram is blocked, a Connection can reach the Bot API through a proxy or through another Bot API address; see
[Telegram in restricted networks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md).

## Join the discussion group and mute the channel

For the people on call:

- **Join the discussion group, and mute the channel itself.** Telegram copies every channel post into the discussion
  group, so each new Alert Group reaches the members of the group once, through its copy, with the Thread of its
  replies under it.
- Only members of the discussion group are notified about the replies in a Thread — even a reply that mentions them.
  Someone who only subscribed to the channel sees the Root messages, but not what happens to them later.

## Known limitation: Quiet Root messages ring the group

A Quiet Root message is sent with `disable_notification`, which in Telegram silences the notification but does not
remove it. Members of the discussion group still get a notification **with sound** for every new Alert Group, because
Telegram notifies them about the copy of the post in the group, and that copy cannot be sent without sound.

## What Muster sends

- The Root message is a regular message in Telegram's HTML: the status and `#N` with the title, linked to the Alert
  Group page, the labels in an expandable quote, the summary, one line per Alert — never a table, which phones cannot
  show — the link to Muster and the footer. Alert data are escaped, so a label value cannot format the message or
  mention anyone. A message is at most 4,096 characters: a long one drops its Alert lines first, then the label
  sections, but always keeps its title, status, footer, buttons and link to Muster.
- Every edit of the Root message carries all its buttons again, because Telegram removes the buttons of a message
  edited without them. The bot may edit its own messages at any age.
- Muster never replies inside the channel: a reply there would be a new post that notifies every subscriber.
- The bot token never appears in a log line, an error, the Timeline or a metric: logs show the scheme and host of the
  Bot API address only, and the token in a request path is written as `bot[redacted]`.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md -->
# Telegram in restricted networks

Muster talks to Telegram only by calling out to the Bot API, `https://api.telegram.org` by default. Where the network
of your installation cannot reach it — Telegram is blocked, or the cluster has no direct way out — there are three
ways to reach it. Use them in this order:

1. [A proxy on the Connection](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md#1-a-proxy-on-the-connection), when a proxy can reach Telegram.
2. [A reverse proxy under your own domain](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md#2-a-reverse-proxy-under-your-own-domain), when you run a host that can
   reach Telegram.
3. [A self-hosted Bot API server](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram-restricted-networks.md#3-a-self-hosted-bot-api-server), only when neither of the first two works. It has
   sharp edges that the first two avoid.

All three keep the bot in Telegram's cloud or move it to one server you control; none needs a change to the
Destinations.

## 1. A proxy on the Connection

Each Connection may send its requests through its own proxy, while the rest of Muster — other Connections, the
identity provider, outgoing webhooks — keeps its own path. On the Connection page, under **Proxy**, turn on
**Use a proxy** and set:

- **Type**: HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5;
- **Address**: `host:port` of the proxy;
- **Username** and **Password**, if the proxy asks for them. The password is stored encrypted and never shown again.

Leave the **Bot API base URL** at `https://api.telegram.org`: the HTTPS connection to Telegram runs through the proxy
end to end, so the proxy never sees the bot token in the request path. Press **Check connection**: every step shows
its latency and whether it went "through the proxy" or "direct", and a proxy that refuses Muster's credentials is
named as such. Pressed before you save a new proxy, the check sends the stored token nowhere and makes only the dry
probe through it, unless you type the bot token again (see [Check before saving](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram.md#check-before-saving)).

The proxy's own address is checked by the Organization's outbound address policy (**Outbound addresses**,
`/admin/organization/outbound`) like any other target: the standard policy allows private addresses and blocks
loopback; the strict policy blocks a proxy on a private address unless an allowed network covers it. `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` are never
read; the proxy is set only on the Connection.

## 2. A reverse proxy under your own domain

When a host that you run can reach `api.telegram.org` — for example a small virtual machine in another network — put
a reverse proxy on it, under a name of your installation's own domain such as `tg.muster.example.org`, in front of
`api.telegram.org`. Muster then calls your domain, and only that host talks to Telegram.

The reverse proxy must:

- connect to `api.telegram.org` over HTTPS with the upstream **SNI** and the **`Host`** header set to
  `api.telegram.org`;
- allow the upstream to answer for longer than the long-polling timeout. In the long polling update mode, Muster asks
  Telegram to hold each `getUpdates` request open for up to 25 seconds and waits up to 35 seconds for the answer; give
  the proxy timeouts of 60 seconds;
- limit the request **body size**. Muster sends no files, only messages of at most 4,096 characters and their
  buttons, so 1 MB is plenty;
- turn the **access log** off, or write it without the request URI: every request path carries the bot token, as in
  `/bot123456789:AA…/sendMessage`;
- answer only Muster: put everything under a **secret path prefix**, a long random string that is never logged, and
  refuse every other path, or allow only Muster's egress addresses with an address **allowlist**, or both.

Then set the Connection's **Bot API base URL** to the reverse proxy, with the prefix:
`https://tg.muster.example.org/8f1c2e…`. Muster sends its requests to `<base>/bot<token>/<method>`. A new base URL
needs the bot token again, so that the stored token never reaches an address you did not mean; type it again and press
**Check connection** before you save: the check runs its three steps against the new address with the typed token;
without the token it makes only the dry probe there (see [Check before saving](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram.md#check-before-saving)). Its
first step is a dry probe, `GET <base>/bot0:x/getMe` without your token, which
`api.telegram.org` answers with `401` and JSON: it tells a wrong host, a wrong path prefix or a server that is not a
Bot API apart before your token goes anywhere. Use an `https` base URL; with `http`, Muster warns that the token
travels in clear text.

### nginx

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name tg.muster.example.org;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/tg.muster.example.org.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/tg.muster.example.org.key;

    # Every request path carries the bot token.
    access_log off;
    client_max_body_size 1m;

    # The secret path prefix; replace it with your own long random string.
    location /8f1c2e…/ {
        # An address allowlist instead of, or besides, the prefix:
        # allow 203.0.113.0/28;
        # deny all;

        proxy_pass https://api.telegram.org/;
        proxy_ssl_server_name on;
        proxy_ssl_name api.telegram.org;
        proxy_ssl_verify on;
        proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt;
        proxy_set_header Host api.telegram.org;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        # Above the long-polling timeout of getUpdates.
        proxy_connect_timeout 10s;
        proxy_send_timeout 60s;
        proxy_read_timeout 60s;
    }

    location / {
        return 404;
    }
}
```

`proxy_pass` with a trailing `/` strips the prefix, so Telegram receives `/bot<token>/<method>`. nginx's error log
names the request of a failed upstream call too; keep it where only administrators can read it.

### Caddy

```caddy
tg.muster.example.org {
    # Caddy writes no access log unless the site has a log directive: leave it out.
    request_body {
        max_size 1MB
    }

    # The secret path prefix; replace it with your own long random string.
    handle_path /8f1c2e…/* {
        # An address allowlist instead of, or besides, the prefix:
        # @outside not remote_ip 203.0.113.0/28
        # respond @outside 404

        reverse_proxy https://api.telegram.org {
            header_up Host api.telegram.org
            transport http {
                tls_server_name api.telegram.org
                # Above the long-polling timeout of getUpdates.
                dial_timeout 10s
                response_header_timeout 60s
            }
        }
    }

    handle {
        respond 404
    }
}
```

`handle_path` strips the prefix before the request goes upstream. Caddy gets and renews the certificate of
`tg.muster.example.org` itself. Caddy's error log entries carry the request URI, with the token, when an upstream
call fails; keep that log where only administrators can read it.

## 3. A self-hosted Bot API server

Telegram publishes the source of its Bot API server
([tdlib/telegram-bot-api](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api)), and a bot can be moved to a server you run.
That server connects to Telegram's data centres itself, over Telegram's own protocol, not through `api.telegram.org`;
it needs a direct route to them (its `--proxy` option applies only to the webhook requests it sends, not to its
connection to Telegram). Use it only when neither a proxy nor a reverse proxy works: it changes
where the bot lives, and every warning below applies.

- **It needs an `api_id` and an `api_hash`.** The server starts only with `--api-id` and `--api-hash`, which you
  register at [my.telegram.org](https://my.telegram.org) with a personal Telegram account. Use a **dedicated** account
  for it, not a person's own: the server's access depends on that account.
- **A bot lives on one server at a time.** While it is on your server, Telegram's cloud does not serve it, and the
  other way round. Every installation and every script that uses the token must use the same server.
- **`logOut` drops unread updates, and the way back to the cloud is closed for 10 minutes.** Moving a bot off the
  cloud starts with `logOut` on `api.telegram.org`. Updates that Muster has not fetched by then — button presses and
  messages of the discussion group — are lost, and after `logOut` the bot cannot log in to the cloud again for
  10 minutes.
- **Any request with the bot's token to `api.telegram.org` moves the bot back to the cloud, silently.** Even a `getMe`
  from a script or a health check on another host is enough. Muster keeps sending to your server, which no longer
  receives the bot's updates: button presses and messages of the discussion group go missing without an error. Never call
  `api.telegram.org` with this token from anywhere while the bot is on your server.
- **The server has no authentication of its own.** Anyone who reaches it can use it with any bot token. Never expose
  it to the internet or to networks other than Muster's; put it on a private address that only the replicas reach.
- **Tokens are visible on its statistics port.** `--http-stat-port` serves statistics that include the bots' tokens.
  Leave it off, or bind it to loopback with `--http-stat-ip-address 127.0.0.1` so that it stays local.
- **Do not use `--local`.** In local mode the server accepts local paths and `file://` URIs in requests and answers
  with absolute paths of its own disk, so anyone who reaches it can make it serve the server's files. Muster sends
  and receives no files and needs none of it.
- **There are no releases.** The project publishes no releases or tags, and container images built from it carry no
  version you can rely on. Build your own image, or pin a third-party image by **digest** (`image@sha256:…`), never by
  a tag such as `latest`.
- **Route `MusterDestinationBroken` of Telegram Destinations elsewhere.** When the server stops, every Telegram
  Destination of that bot becomes Broken at once. Route the Internal alert
  [`MusterDestinationBroken`](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterDestinationBroken.md) of Telegram Destinations to a
  Destination that is not in Telegram — Mattermost or an outgoing webhook — and its chart rule around Muster.

The server's address is an ordinary target of the outbound address policy: the standard policy allows a private
address and blocks loopback.

### Move a bot between servers

Muster has no wizard for this; the move is a **manual** procedure. Plan for a short gap in which presses and messages
of the discussion group are lost.

What Muster does with `deleteWebhook`: it calls `deleteWebhook` only when a Connection leaves the webhook update mode
— saved from Webhook to Long polling — and calls it at the base URL saved before, the server the bot is leaving. When
that call fails, the save fails ("deleteWebhook failed: …") and nothing changes. Changing only the base URL while the
Connection stays in the webhook mode calls `setWebhook` at the new base URL and never `deleteWebhook` at the old one.
Deleting a Connection in the webhook mode also calls `deleteWebhook`, best effort, at its saved base URL: the outcome
is logged (`telegram_webhook_deleted` or `telegram_webhook_delete_failed`) and never fails the deletion. Muster never
calls `logOut` or `close`.

From Telegram's cloud to your server:

1. Start the Bot API server as above and check from a replica that it answers:
   `curl -s http://bot-api.internal.example.org:8081/bot0:x/getMe` returns `401` and JSON. The server listens on
   plain HTTP (port 8081 by default); with an `http` base URL Muster warns that the token travels in clear text,
   which is acceptable only on a private network or through a tunnel.
2. If the Connection uses the webhook update mode, switch it to **Long polling** and save **while the old server
   still answers**, so that Muster's own `deleteWebhook` reaches it. If the save fails, fix the path to the old server
   first.
3. Stop every other process that uses the bot's token.
4. Optionally call `deleteWebhook` yourself on the old server, then `logOut`:

    ```sh
    curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot$TOKEN/deleteWebhook"
    curl -s "https://api.telegram.org/bot$TOKEN/logOut"
    ```

    The `deleteWebhook` before `logOut` is a best-effort step: if it fails, go on with `logOut`; it does not stop the
    move.
5. On the Connection, set the **Bot API base URL** to your server, enter the bot token again, and save.
6. Press **Check connection**: the dry probe, then `getMe` and `getWebhookInfo` with your token against the saved
   base URL. Run `muster doctor` too; it checks the saved Connections the same way.
7. Switch back to the webhook update mode if you used it: Muster calls `setWebhook` on your server.

From one server you run to another, use the same steps on the old server, as Telegram documents in
[Moving a bot from one local server to another](https://github.com/tdlib/telegram-bot-api#moving), in one of two ways:

- call `logOut` on the old server instead of on `api.telegram.org`; updates not yet fetched are lost;
- or call `deleteWebhook` and then `close` on the old server, and move the bot's subdirectory — named by the bot's
  user id, the number before the colon in its token — from the old server's working directory to the new server's;
  no updates are lost. `close` answers `429` during the first 10 minutes after the bot started on that server.

Back to Telegram's cloud: the same steps in the other direction — switch to long polling while your server still
answers, `logOut` on your server, then set the base URL back to `https://api.telegram.org` with the token. The cloud
takes the bot back only when 10 minutes have passed since its `logOut` from the cloud.

See also Telegram's [`logOut`](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#logout),
[`close`](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#close) and
[Using a Local Bot API Server](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#using-a-local-bot-api-server).

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md -->
# Connect Slack

Muster posts to Slack through the Web API with the **bot** of a Slack app that you create from a manifest and install in
your workspace: one message per Alert Group, the **Root message**, which Muster edits as the Alert Group changes, and
replies in its **Thread** for what happens later. People act on the Alert Group with the buttons of the message and its
**Snooze…** menu. Muster uses no incoming webhook, no Events API subscription and no user token.

In the examples, `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` is `https://muster.example.org` and `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is
`https://ingest.muster.example.org`.

## Socket Mode or HTTP

A button press reaches Muster in one of two **event modes**, set on the Connection (`connection.slack.event_mode`).
Choose before you create the app, because the app's manifest differs.

Socket Mode
:   The Leader holds a WebSocket connection to Slack, so Slack needs no address of Muster: Muster only calls out. It is
    the way when Muster has no address that Slack can reach. It needs the app-level token. Only the Leader holds the
    socket, so a press made while the Leader changes is lost: the person sees Slack's error, and Muster does not count
    on Slack to send it again. A handover takes well under a minute; see
    [High availability](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/high-availability.md).

HTTP
:   Slack posts every press to the Connection's callback address, which the Connection page shows:

    ```text
    https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/slack/CN…
    ```

    Slack must reach this address over HTTPS. Any replica receives the press, so no press is lost while the Leader
    changes. It needs the app's Slack signing secret: Muster verifies the signature of every press with it, and
    refuses a request whose timestamp is further than `slack.request_tolerance` (5 minutes) from its own clock, so keep
    the clocks of Muster's nodes right. A request with a wrong or missing signature, a stale timestamp, an unknown
    Connection or a Connection in Socket Mode is answered `401` with the same body, which reveals nothing about which
    Connections exist; a body over 1 MiB, or one without a `payload`, is answered `400`.

    If Slack is the only client outside your network that reaches the ingest listener, expose only `/api/v1/callbacks/`
    on the address Slack reaches, for example with a reverse proxy that forwards that path alone to the ingest port.
    `MUSTER_INGEST_URL` is also the address of Alertmanagers and Heartbeats: when they come from outside too, publish
    their paths as well, or give Slack's callbacks a route of their own. See
    [The two public addresses](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/helm.md#the-two-public-addresses).

A Slack app sends its presses to the sockets alone while its Socket Mode is on, and over HTTP alone while it is off, so
the app and the Connection must agree: a Connection receives presses only in its own mode.

### One Slack app per Connection

Slack hands each press to any one of the app's open socket connections, and Muster binds a press to a Destination of
the Connection that receives it. Two Connections on one Slack app, in one Muster or in two, would therefore share its
presses at random, and a press that reaches the wrong Connection is refused as "This button could not be verified".
Over HTTP an app has one Request URL, so it serves one Connection. Create a Slack app for each Connection, a test copy
of Muster included.

Muster notices it. When Slack tells the Leader that the app has more socket connections than the Leader holds, another
program is connected to the same app, usually a second Connection or Muster, or a script: the **Check connection** of a
Connection in Socket Mode passes with the warning `another_client_connected`, the Connection page shows the same
warning, `muster doctor` prints a `WARN` line, and the Leader logs
[`slack_socket_shared`](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/log-events.md#slack_socket_shared). Presses go on working, but some of them are
lost to the other program. Muster takes the count at each `hello`: when a socket reconnects, at the planned refresh
hours after the previous one, and when the Connection is saved with a change, which restarts its socket at once. So the
warning can stay for hours after its cause is gone; to clear it, save the Connection with its app-level token entered
again. How long Slack counts the connection of a Leader that crashed has not been verified.

## Create the app from a manifest

1. Open [Your Apps](https://api.slack.com/apps) in Slack, select **Create New App → From a manifest**, choose the
   workspace and paste one of the manifests below, in YAML.
2. Check the summary Slack shows and create the app.

### The manifest for Socket Mode

```yaml
display_information:
  name: Muster
  description: Muster alert groups
features:
  app_home:
    home_tab_enabled: false
    messages_tab_enabled: true
    messages_tab_read_only_enabled: true
  bot_user:
    display_name: Muster
oauth_config:
  scopes:
    bot:
      - chat:write
      - channels:read
      - groups:read
      - im:write
      - users:read
      - users:read.email
settings:
  interactivity:
    is_enabled: true
  org_deploy_enabled: false
  socket_mode_enabled: true
  token_rotation_enabled: false
```

### The manifest for HTTP

It differs from the first in the Interactivity Request URL, the callback address of the Connection, and in Socket Mode,
which is off:

```yaml
display_information:
  name: Muster
  description: Muster alert groups
features:
  app_home:
    home_tab_enabled: false
    messages_tab_enabled: true
    messages_tab_read_only_enabled: true
  bot_user:
    display_name: Muster
oauth_config:
  scopes:
    bot:
      - chat:write
      - channels:read
      - groups:read
      - im:write
      - users:read
      - users:read.email
settings:
  interactivity:
    is_enabled: true
    request_url: https://ingest.muster.example.org/api/v1/callbacks/slack/CNAGK7M3QX9P2R
  org_deploy_enabled: false
  socket_mode_enabled: false
  token_rotation_enabled: false
```

The Connection page shows its callback address only once the Connection is saved, and saving it needs the bot token of
the installed app. Create the app with the address above, create the Connection, then copy its callback address into
**Interactivity & Shortcuts → Request URL** of the app.

### What the manifest sets

The app and its bot are named **Muster**. The bot posts under the name in the app's settings: Muster does not ask for
`chat:write.customize`, so a name that a message carries would be ignored. To use another name, change both names in
the manifest.

The Messages tab is on and read-only
:   Account links send a person a code by direct message from the bot, and the direct messages of an app show in its
    Messages tab. Read-only means that the person reads the code and cannot write to the bot. Keep the tab on: Slack
    documents that with it off it refuses the bot's direct message, and the request for a code then fails with the
    problem `messages_tab_disabled` (`409`), which has not been seen yet on a real workspace. A refused request still
    counts toward the limits of Account links, 5 requests an hour for a person and 3 for one Slack account
    (`account_link.slack_code_requests`), so after you turn the tab on again, a person who tried several times may have
    to wait up to an hour. Turn it on under **App Home → Show Tabs → Messages Tab**. See [Link
    Slack](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md#link-slack).

The Home tab is off
:   Muster publishes no Home tab.

Interactivity is on
:   Buttons and menus send nothing to Muster without it. Over HTTP it holds the Request URL.

Socket Mode is on, or off for HTTP
:   See [Socket Mode or HTTP](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md#socket-mode-or-http).

Token rotation is off
:   With rotation, the bot token expires and Slack issues a new one. Muster stores the token you enter and has no way to
    renew it, so a rotating token ends as `token_expired` and every Destination of the Connection becomes
    [Broken](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md).

The app is not deployed to an organization
:   One Connection serves one app in one workspace.

There is no event subscription
:   Muster does not use the Events API: it hears only the presses of buttons and menus.

### The scopes

Muster needs these six bot scopes and no other. **Check connection** reads the scopes Slack grants the token and fails
with `missing_scope`, naming the missing ones.

`chat:write`
:   Posts, edits and deletes the bot's own messages, and answers the people who press its buttons.

`channels:read`
:   Reads a public channel to check a Destination, and lists the public channels the bot is a member of.

`groups:read`
:   The same for private channels.

`im:write`
:   Lets the bot open a direct chat with a person. The Connection check fails without it. The code of an Account link
    is sent with `chat.postMessage` to the person's user id, which needs `chat:write`; whether Slack also needs
    `im:write` for that has not been verified, so Muster keeps the scope.

`users:read`
:   Finds a person by name for an Account link, and reads the app of the bot so that the check can tell whether both
    tokens belong to one app.

`users:read.email`
:   Finds a person by email for an Account link.

Muster never joins a channel on its own, so it asks for no `channels:join`: you invite the bot.

## Install the app and create the tokens

1. In the app's settings, open **Install App** and install it in the workspace. Slack then shows the **Bot User OAuth
   Token** under **OAuth & Permissions**; it starts with `xoxb-`. Copy it. Anyone with the token controls the bot.
2. In Socket Mode, open **Basic Information → App-Level Tokens** and generate a token with the scope
   `connections:write`. It starts with `xapp-`. Copy it. Anyone with this token can open sockets of the app and take
   its presses.
3. Over HTTP, open **Basic Information → App Credentials** and copy the **Signing Secret**. Anyone with it can send
   Muster presses that pass the signature check.
