   ```python
               self.send_response(401); self.end_headers(); return
           event = json.loads(body)
           wid = self.headers["webhook-id"]
           if wid not in seen and event["notify"] and event["event"] in CALL_ON:
               group = event["alert_group"]
               call = urllib.request.Request(
                   os.environ["PROVIDER_URL"],          # your provider's HTTP API
                   json.dumps({"to": os.environ["ON_CALL_NUMBER"],
                               "text": f"Muster #{group['number']}: {group['title']}"}).encode(),
                   {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["PROVIDER_TOKEN"],
                    "Content-Type": "application/json"})
               urllib.request.urlopen(call, timeout=10)  # an error here fails the request, and Muster retries the same event
               seen.add(wid)
           self.send_response(204); self.end_headers()

   HTTPServer(("", 8080), Relay).serve_forever()
   ```

What to know:

- **Which events.** `created` is a new Alert Group, `ack_timeout` a notice that nobody took it, and `reopened` a problem
  that returned. Leave out `alerts_added` and `reminder`, which are Loud too but only worth a message. The relay can
  also skip an Alert Group that is already acknowledged: every event carries the Alert Group's `status` as it was when
  the event was recorded.
- **Answer honestly.** `2xx` marks the event delivered. A `5xx` makes Muster send the same event again with the same
  `webhook-id`. A `400` or `422` drops that one event. `401`, `403`, `404` and `410` make the Destination
  [Broken](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md), which is right for a relay that is misconfigured. See [How the answer
  counts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/events.md#how-the-answer-counts).
- **Test it.** **Send test message** sends the event `test` with `notify` false. For the first run, add `"test"` to
  `CALL_ON` and replace `event["notify"]` in the condition with `(event["notify"] or event["event"] == "test")`, then
  change both back.

## A status page

**Mode: template.** A status page that has an HTTP API takes one incident per problem and lets you update it. That is the
shape of the template mode: `create` opens the incident and extracts its id from the answer, and `update` changes it to
the current state.

This sketch uses the incident API of the open status page Cachet 2.x as the example: a `POST` to `/api/v1/incidents`
answers `{"data": {"id": 7, …}}`, and a `PUT` to `/api/v1/incidents/7` changes it. Its `status` is 1 for investigating, 2
for identified and 4 for fixed. Create a Secret `token` with the page's API token.

`create`:

```
POST https://status.example.org/api/v1/incidents
X-Cachet-Token: {{ .Secrets.token }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"name": {{ .AlertGroup.Title | toJson }},
 "message": {{ .AlertGroup.Summary | toJson }},
 "status": 1,
 "visible": 1}
```

Extraction rule: the name `id`, the path `$.data.id`.

`update`:

```
PUT https://status.example.org/api/v1/incidents/{{ .Response.id }}
X-Cachet-Token: {{ .Secrets.token }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"name": {{ .AlertGroup.Title | toJson }},
 "message": {{ .AlertGroup.Summary | toJson }},
 "status": {{ if eq .AlertGroup.Status "resolved" }}4{{ else if eq .AlertGroup.Status "firing" }}1{{ else }}2{{ end }},
 "visible": 1}
```

The incident opens as investigating when an Alert Group appears, becomes identified while somebody has it or it is
snoozed, and becomes fixed when the Alert Group resolves. If the Alert Group reopens, the next `update` says investigating
again.

Think before you publish: the title and summary of an Alert Group come from your alert rules and may show internal names.
Use a Route with Matchers for the alerts that are meant for your users, and write the summary annotations for them.

## A second chat

**Mode: template.** A chat with an open REST API and incoming messages is a Destination of its own: the same Alert Groups,
in a second place. The template mode keeps one message per Alert Group in it, edits it where the chat's API allows, and
posts the replies of the Thread.

This sketch uses the REST API of Rocket.Chat as the example. A `POST` to `chat.postMessage` answers with the message under
`message`, with its `_id` and its room id `rid`; `chat.update` edits it; a message with a `tmid` is a reply in its thread.
Create the Secrets `token` and `user_id` for the bot user's token and id.

`create`:

```
POST https://chat.example.org/api/v1/chat.postMessage
X-Auth-Token: {{ .Secrets.token }}
X-User-Id: {{ .Secrets.user_id }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"channel": "#alerts",
 "text": {{ printf "#%d %s (%s)\n%s" .AlertGroup.Number .AlertGroup.Title .AlertGroup.Status .AlertGroup.URL | toJson }}}
```

Extraction rules: `id` with `$.message._id`, and `room` with `$.message.rid`.

`update`:

```
POST https://chat.example.org/api/v1/chat.update
X-Auth-Token: {{ .Secrets.token }}
X-User-Id: {{ .Secrets.user_id }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"roomId": {{ .Response.room | toJson }},
 "msgId": {{ .Response.id | toJson }},
 "text": {{ printf "#%d %s (%s)\n%s" .AlertGroup.Number .AlertGroup.Title .AlertGroup.Status .AlertGroup.URL | toJson }}}
```

`reply_in_thread`:

```
POST https://chat.example.org/api/v1/chat.postMessage
X-Auth-Token: {{ .Secrets.token }}
X-User-Id: {{ .Secrets.user_id }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"roomId": {{ .Response.room | toJson }},
 "tmid": {{ .Response.id | toJson }},
 "text": {{ printf "%s on #%d" .Event .AlertGroup.Number | toJson }}}
```

What to know:

- **Edits may be limited by the chat.** Many chats let a user edit a message only for a while, or not at all. If yours does,
  the `update` of an old message is refused, and by the chat's answer that ends as Not delivered or makes the Destination
  Broken. Check the chat's setting for editing messages. If you
  cannot allow edits, make `update` a second `chat.postMessage` call: each change is then a new message instead of an
  edit.
- **Loud and Quiet.** A chat decides for itself what rings. Muster tells the template through `.Notify`, and through
  `.Mentions` whom to mention; wrap them in the chat's syntax with the `mention` function, as [Mentions](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/templates.md#mentions)
  shows.
- **Two-step threads.** A chat that needs a thread created first uses `open_thread`; see [Recipe: a chat with two-step
  threads](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/templates.md#recipe-a-chat-with-two-step-threads).

## An issue tracker

**Mode: template.** Opening an issue when a problem starts, commenting on it as it develops, and closing it when the
problem resolves needs one thing: the id of the issue that the first request created, in every later request. That is what
the extraction rules are for. The `create` request opens the issue and extracts its number, `update` changes its state,
and `reply_in_thread` adds comments.

This sketch uses the issue API of the open forges Gitea and Forgejo, which share it. A `POST` to
`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` answers with the issue, including its `number`; a `PATCH` to
`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}` changes its `state` to `open` or `closed`; a `POST` to
`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}/comments` adds a comment. Create a Secret `token` with an access token of a bot user
that may write issues in the repository.

`create`:

```
POST https://git.example.org/api/v1/repos/ops/alerts/issues
Authorization: token {{ .Secrets.token }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"title": {{ printf "#%d %s" .AlertGroup.Number .AlertGroup.Title | toJson }},
 "body": {{ printf "%s\n\n%s" .AlertGroup.Summary .AlertGroup.URL | toJson }}}
```

Extraction rule: the name `number`, the path `$.number`.

`update`:

```
PATCH https://git.example.org/api/v1/repos/ops/alerts/issues/{{ .Response.number }}
Authorization: token {{ .Secrets.token }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"title": {{ printf "#%d %s (%s)" .AlertGroup.Number .AlertGroup.Title .AlertGroup.Status | toJson }},
 "state": "{{ if eq .AlertGroup.Status "resolved" }}closed{{ else }}open{{ end }}"}
```

`reply_in_thread`:

```
POST https://git.example.org/api/v1/repos/ops/alerts/issues/{{ .Response.number }}/comments
Authorization: token {{ .Secrets.token }}
Content-Type: application/json
```

```
{"body": {{ printf "%s: %s" .Event .AlertGroup.URL | toJson }}}
```

The issue opens with the Alert Group, gets a comment for each Thread reply, such as new Alerts, a Takeover or a Reminder,
closes when the Alert Group is resolved, and opens again if the Alert Group returns. The title shows the current status.

What to know:

- **One issue per Alert Group.** A Route that takes many Alert Groups opens many issues. Narrow its Matchers, or choose a
  Group key that groups more.
- **If the extraction finds nothing,** the `create` still counts as delivered, the Timeline records the missing value, and
  every later request that reads it fails as a template error. Check the answer in the **Send test message** result,
  sent to a test repository.
- **A tracker whose answer carries no id** cannot be driven this way. Use the events mode with a relay that remembers the
  id of the issue for each `alert_group.id`, and does what the recipe above does with the events `created`, `resolved` and
  `reopened`.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/index.md -->
# Sign-in

Everything in the web UI and the API works only after sign-in. No page and no read of the API is open to someone who has
not signed in. What is open is a short list of endpoints that cannot ask for a session:

- the sign-in itself: the list of sign-in methods, the password sign-in, the OpenID Connect redirect and its callback,
  and the page where a person sets a password from a setup link;
- [ingestion](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md) and the [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md), which take an
  Integration token;
- the callbacks that Mattermost, Slack, Telegram and a [Bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/bridge.md) send to Muster, which each
  carry a secret or a signature of their own;
- the served API specification;
- the health checks and `/metrics`, on the internal listener, which is not meant to be reachable from outside the
  cluster.

Everything else answers `401` without a session or a token.

## Roles

Each User and Service account has one of three Roles, each a fixed set of Permissions:

| Role | May |
|---|---|
| Admin | everything: also configures Integrations, Routes, Connections and Destinations, manages Users, the OIDC settings, Service accounts, the Organization's settings, and reads the Audit log and the System status |
| Responder | what a Viewer reads, and acts on Alert Groups: acknowledges and takes over, resolves, snoozes, adds Notes and answers Reminders |
| Viewer | reads Alert Groups, Alerts, Integrations, Routes, Connections, Destinations, Link rules and Lookup tables, with secret values masked |

Every signed-in person also manages their own profile: password, TOTP, Account links and Personal access tokens. Every operation in the [API reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/api.md) names the Permission it needs.

## Ways to sign in

- **Local users.** An Admin creates a user with a login, and Muster returns a single-use link, valid for 24 hours
  (`auth.password_setup_link_ttl`), where the person sets a password of at least 12 characters
  (`auth.password_min_length`). Muster sends no email; the Admin hands the link over. The first Admin comes from
  `MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` and its password at the first start, as the [Quick start](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/quick-start.md) shows.
- **OpenID Connect.** People sign in at your identity provider, and a mapping from the groups in their token to Roles
  decides what they may do. [Sign-in with Keycloak](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/oidc-keycloak.md) is a complete walkthrough.
- **TOTP.** A second step with a one-time code from an authenticator app, for local and OIDC users alike; the
  Organization can require it. See [TOTP](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/totp.md).
- **Personal access tokens.** A person creates them in the profile for scripts. A token acts as its User, with at most
  that User's Permissions, and can be narrowed to fewer. It can expire (`token.expiry`; a token has no expiry unless
  you set one, and the page warns about that), and the Audit log names the token with the person. The API limits each
  token (`api.rate_limit`). See [API tokens and automation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/configure/api-tokens.md).
- **Service accounts.** An identity that is not a person, for automation such as a pipeline. It has a Role and any number
  of tokens, cannot sign in to the web UI, and cannot become the Owner of an Alert Group.

Operations that change one's own account, such as the password, TOTP, tokens and Account links, need the web session; a
token is refused there.

A web session ends after 12 hours without a request (`auth.session_idle_timeout`), or 7 days after sign-in
(`auth.session_lifetime`). Both are built in. A session of an OIDC user whose identity provider granted no offline token
ends 12 hours after sign-in (`auth.oidc_fallback_session_lifetime`), and a background re-check asks the identity provider
about every OIDC user who has an offline token and a live session or a usable Personal access token, every 15 minutes
(`auth.oidc_recheck_interval`).

When the identity provider is in a network that Muster cannot reach, see [Closed networks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/closed-networks.md).

## Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost

The session cookie is `Secure`, so browsers keep it only on a page served over HTTPS or from the browser's own machine:
`localhost`, a name under `.localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`. On plain `http://` to any other address, such as
`http://192.0.2.10:8080`, the browser drops the cookie and every sign-in returns to the sign-in page. Muster says so in
two places:

- the sign-in page shows "Sign-in needs HTTPS or localhost" above the form when the browser does not treat the page as
  secure;
- the server logs [`public_url_insecure`](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/log-events.md#public_url_insecure) at WARN when it starts with
  `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` set to an `http://` address on any other host.

There are two ways out:

- **HTTPS.** Put a reverse proxy or an [Ingress](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/helm.md#ingress) with a certificate in front of the app
  port 8080, set `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` to its `https://` address and restart Muster.
- **An SSH tunnel to localhost**, to try Muster on another machine without a certificate. On your own machine, run
  `ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 <host>`, keep it open and browse to `http://localhost:8080`, with `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL`
  set to `http://localhost:8080`. Safari may drop the cookie on `localhost` too: if sign-in still returns to the
  sign-in page there, use HTTPS or another browser.

## Link your messenger accounts

A button in Mattermost, Slack or Telegram acts as a Muster User only if the person who presses it has linked their
messenger account to their User. People do it themselves, from their profile, as [Link your messenger
accounts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md) describes. Admins cannot do it for them: they see the links of every User and
can remove them, but they cannot create one for someone else. A press from an unlinked account changes nothing, and the
person is answered privately with a link to their profile.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/oidc-keycloak.md -->
# Sign-in with Keycloak

This page sets up sign-in through [Keycloak](https://www.keycloak.org/) with OpenID Connect (OIDC). Other identity
providers work the same way: Muster needs a confidential client with the authorization code flow, a claim that lists
the person's groups, and, for the background re-checks, the scope `offline_access`.

Muster talks to Keycloak over the **back channel**: it fetches the provider metadata (discovery) and the signing keys,
and exchanges the authorization code for tokens itself. Muster must therefore reach Keycloak over the network, directly
or through the proxy of the OIDC settings. If it cannot — Keycloak sits in a closed network and Muster outside it — use
[local users with TOTP](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/oidc-keycloak.md#when-muster-cannot-reach-the-identity-provider) instead.

In the examples, Keycloak runs at `https://keycloak.example.org` with the realm `ops`, and `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` is
`https://muster.example.org`.

## 1. Create the client

In the Keycloak admin console, open the realm, then **Clients → Create client**:

<!-- tablecheck: allow the names fit; the long values are URLs to copy, longer than a phone line in any layout -->

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Client type | OpenID Connect |
| Client ID | `muster` |
| Client authentication | On (a confidential client with a client secret) |
| Authentication flow | **Standard flow** only; switch off Direct access grants, Implicit flow and Service accounts |
| Valid redirect URIs | `https://muster.example.org/api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback` and `https://muster.example.org/api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback` |
| Web origins | leave empty: the browser never calls Keycloak from Muster's pages |

Both redirect URIs are `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` followed by a path: `/api/v1/sessions/oidc/callback` ends a sign-in, and
`/api/v1/me/oidc-identity/callback` ends linking an existing account to Keycloak from its profile. Register both, with
exactly the scheme, host and port of `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL`.

Under **Advanced → Advanced settings**, set **Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method** to `S256`. Muster
always sends a PKCE challenge, so this only makes Keycloak insist on it.

Then open **Credentials** and copy the **Client secret**. Note when it expires, if your realm rotates client secrets:
Muster warns two weeks before the date you enter (`oidc.secret_expiry_lead`).

## 2. Add the groups claim

Muster gives each person a Role from their groups. Keycloak puts groups into tokens only through a mapper:

1. Open the client → **Client scopes** → `muster-dedicated` → **Add mapper → By configuration → Group Membership**.
2. Set **Name** to `groups` and **Token Claim Name** to `groups`.
3. Switch **Full group path** off, so that the claim carries `oncall` rather than `/oncall`.
4. Switch on **Add to ID token** and **Add to userinfo**.

Muster reads the groups from the ID token, and from the userinfo endpoint when the ID token lacks the claim; the
userinfo answer must be plain JSON, not a signed JWT. The name of the claim is the **Groups claim** of the OIDC
settings; it is `groups` unless you change both.

## 3. Allow `offline_access`

Muster asks for the scope `offline_access` at every sign-in, besides the scopes of the settings. With it, Keycloak
returns an offline token, which Muster keeps encrypted and uses to **re-check every OIDC user in the background**
every 15 minutes (`auth.oidc_recheck_interval`): a person disabled or removed in Keycloak loses their Muster sessions
at the next re-check, without waiting for them to end.

To allow it:

1. Make sure the realm role `offline_access` is a default role of the realm (**Realm settings → User registration →
   Default roles**), which it is in a new realm, or give it to the groups that use Muster.
2. Open the client → **Client scopes** and check that the client scope `offline_access` is assigned as **Optional**.

### Without `offline_access`

Sign-in still works when Keycloak does not grant `offline_access`, but Muster cannot re-check the person in the
background:

- there are no background re-checks for them;
- each of their OIDC sessions ends `auth.oidc_fallback_session_lifetime` (12 hours) after sign-in, even while in use,
  so that a person disabled in Keycloak is signed out within that time;
- their Personal access tokens work only while their last OIDC sign-in is within `auth.oidc_token_grace` (7 days);
  after that, the tokens are refused until they sign in through OIDC again.

## 4. Configure Muster

Sign in to Muster as an Admin and open **OIDC settings**, or use `PUT /api/v1/oidc-settings`:

<!-- tablecheck: allow the names fit; the long values are URLs to copy, longer than a phone line in any layout -->

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuer URL | `https://keycloak.example.org/realms/ops` — the `issuer` of `https://keycloak.example.org/realms/ops/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Use `https`: over `http` the client secret and the tokens cross the network in clear text |
| Client ID | `muster` |
| Client secret | the secret of step 1; it is write-only: Muster shows only whether it is set and when it changed |
| Client secret expires on | the expiry date of the secret, if it has one |
| Display name | the name on the button "Sign in with {name}"; by default the host of the issuer URL |
| Scopes | `profile email`; `openid` and `offline_access` are always added |
| Groups claim | `groups` |
| Group mapping | for example `muster-admins` → Admin, `oncall` → Responder; when a person's groups map to several Roles, the highest wins |
| Role for users without a matching group | none (the default) refuses their sign-in; Viewer or Responder lets them in |
| Sync Role at sign-in | on (the default): Keycloak decides the Role at every sign-in and re-check; off: the mapping applies only when the user is created |
| Skip TOTP when the IdP asserted MFA | off by default; on skips Muster's own TOTP step when the ID token's `amr` claim says that Keycloak used multi-factor authentication. Keycloak sends `amr` only when the client has an *Authentication Method Reference (AMR)* mapper |
| Proxy | the HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5 proxy through which Muster reaches Keycloak, if it needs one |

The settings behind the three rows above Proxy are `oidc.unmatched_role` (none: sign-in is refused), `oidc.sync_role`
(on) and
`oidc.skip_totp_with_idp_mfa` (off).

Then press **Check connection**. The check fetches discovery through the saved settings and proxy and shows how the
request travelled (`direct` or `proxy`), how long it took and the endpoints Keycloak announced. When the outbound
address policy blocks Keycloak or the proxy, the error names the rule.

Keycloak lists only standard claims in `claims_supported`, so the check shows the warning *Nobody will be able to sign
in through OIDC* (`groups_claim_missing`) although the mapper of step 2 exists. The warning goes away at the first
sign-in whose token carries the groups claim. If it stays, the mapper is missing or not added to the ID token.

The settings also warn when the mapping is empty and users without a matching group get no Role
(`nobody_can_sign_in`), and two weeks before the client secret expires.

## 5. Sign in

Open Muster and press **Sign in with {display name}**. The first sign-in of a person creates their Muster user with
the Role of their groups. The login is Keycloak's `preferred_username`, else the email, else the subject. Muster never
merges accounts by login or email: when a local user already has the login, the sign-in is refused with "An account
with this login already exists. Sign in with it and link OIDC in your profile."

A person whose groups map to no Role is refused with "You have no access to Muster. Contact your administrator.", and
the Audit log entry `session.oidc_refused` lists the groups their token carried. A user with TOTP gives the code after
Keycloak, unless Keycloak asserted multi-factor authentication and the setting above skips it.

Other errors on the sign-in page: `account_disabled` (the Muster user is disabled or deleted), `oidc_disabled` (OIDC
was switched off), `invalid_request` (the sign-in took longer than 10 minutes, `oidc.auth_request_ttl`, or was
started in another browser) and `idp_error` (Keycloak reported an error, could not be reached, or answered with a
token that did not verify; the log event `oidc_sign_in_failed` says which).

## When Muster cannot reach the identity provider

OIDC needs the back channel from Muster to Keycloak. When Keycloak is inside a closed network that Muster cannot
reach, even through a proxy, use local users instead:

- an Admin creates each user and hands over the one-time password setup link (**Users → Create**);
- set **Organization → Security → TOTP required** to *everyone*, so that every user enrols TOTP at their first sign-in.

Local sign-in is always available, also next to OIDC, and the bootstrap Admin or `muster admin reset-password --actor
<name>` lets an operator in when the OIDC settings are broken.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/totp.md -->
# TOTP

TOTP is a second step in the sign-in: a six-digit code from an authenticator app, which changes every 30 seconds
([RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238)). Every User, local or from OpenID Connect, can enrol it. It adds
protection to a password that leaks, and it is the second factor of installations that cannot use an identity provider:
see [Closed networks](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/closed-networks.md).

## Enrol

People enrol from their **profile**: they scan a QR code with the authenticator app and confirm with the first code.
Enrolment gives the person **10 recovery codes** (`auth.totp_recovery_codes`), each of ten characters and usable once. They are shown **once**:
save them somewhere safe. In the profile a person can generate new recovery codes, which replace the unused ones, and
remove TOTP. Removing it needs the current password (a local user) or a current code or recovery code.

A User has one enrolment. From then on, every sign-in asks for a code after the password, or after the redirect from the
identity provider. A recovery code is accepted in place of a code, and is then used up. Until the code is given, the
session can only read itself, sign out and give the code.

A wrong password or code counts as a failure, and failures slow the next attempts down per account and per source
address: after 3 in a row, each attempt waits twice as long as the one before, from 1 second up to 60 seconds.

## The policy

The Organization's policy **TOTP required** (`organization.totp_required`), under Organization → Security, has three
values:

| Value | Who must have TOTP |
|---|---|
| nobody (the default) | no one; everyone may enrol if they want |
| local users | every account that has a password |
| everyone | every account, local or from OpenID Connect |

A person who falls under the policy and has no TOTP yet must enrol right after sign-in, before they can do anything
else. An account that signs in through OpenID Connect, whether created by it or linked to it, does not count as a local
user for this policy.

## OpenID Connect and the identity provider's multi-factor authentication

An identity provider may already ask for a second factor. When the OIDC setting `oidc.skip_totp_with_idp_mfa` (skip TOTP when the identity provider
asserted multi-factor authentication; off by default) is on, Muster skips its own code
for a sign-in where the provider's token says so in its `amr` claim. With the setting off, Muster asks for its own code
whenever the User has TOTP. See [Sign-in with Keycloak](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/oidc-keycloak.md).

## A lost authenticator

A person who lost both the device and the recovery codes needs a reset.

- **An Admin** resets it under **Access** → **Users**: **Reset TOTP**.
- **From the command line**, when no Admin can sign in:

  ```sh
  muster admin reset-totp --actor ops-alice alice
  ```

  `--actor` names the person who runs the command, and is required; the last argument is the login of the account. The
  command works on the database, with the same settings as the server.

A reset removes the TOTP and its recovery codes and ends the account's sessions. Under a policy that covers the account,
the person enrols again at the next sign-in. Without the policy, they can enrol again from the profile.

## What the Audit log records

The Audit log, under Organization → Audit log, records TOTP enrolled, removed and reset, with the User, who did it, and
the Transport (`cli` for the command). It never records a code. Failed sign-ins, with a wrong code too, are counted in
the metric `muster_login_failures_total` with the method `totp`; the chart rule `MusterLoginFailures` watches it.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/closed-networks.md -->
# Closed networks

OpenID Connect needs a **back channel**: Muster itself calls the identity provider, to read its configuration and keys,
to exchange the code for tokens, and to check the sessions again later. Where Muster is outside the network of the
identity provider and cannot reach it, OpenID Connect cannot work, even though the people's browsers can. Typical cases
are an identity provider inside a company network and Muster in a cloud or a different site.

If a proxy can bring Muster to the provider, set it in the OIDC settings first: see [Proxies](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/proxies.md).
When it cannot, use **local users with TOTP**. The [Keycloak page](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/oidc-keycloak.md#when-muster-cannot-reach-the-identity-provider)
describes the symptoms of an unreachable provider and does not repeat them here.

## Set it up

1. Sign in as the bootstrap Admin, whose email and password come from `MUSTER_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL` and its password
   variable at the first start.
2. Under **Access** → **Users**, create a user for each person, with a login and a Role.
3. Hand each person the one-time setup link that Muster shows. It is valid for 24 hours and works once. Muster sends no
   email, so you pass it on yourself. The person sets a password of at least 12 characters.
4. Under Organization → Security, set **TOTP required** to **local users**, or to **everyone**. With the policy, the
   person enrols [TOTP](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/totp.md) right after the first sign-in and saves the 10 recovery codes. Without it, the policy
   would only be a wish: enrolment would be each person's choice.
5. Add [Personal access tokens](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/index.md#ways-to-sign-in) for scripts and Service accounts for automation. They do not
   depend on the identity provider.

Take care of the way back: keep at least two Admins, and keep the recovery codes of each. If the last Admin loses the
second factor, `muster admin reset-totp --actor <name> <login>` resets it from the command line, and
`muster admin reset-password --actor <name> <login>` sets a new password.

Local sign-in and OpenID Connect can run side by side. If the provider becomes reachable later, configure OIDC and let
people link it from their profile; their TOTP stays.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md -->
# Alert Groups

An **Alert Group** is a set of Alerts that Muster treats as one problem. It is the thing people act on: it has a number
like `#412`, a status, and at most one **Owner**, and each Destination that receives it shows it as a single message
that Muster keeps up to date. Acknowledge it, snooze it or resolve it, and everyone looking at it sees the result.

This page explains what an Alert Group is and how it relates to the other things Muster handles. The pages that follow
go deeper:

- [Routes and Group keys](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md): how an Alert finds its Alert Group.
- [Snapshot semantics](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md): how Alertmanager's notifications become Alerts, and when an Alert counts
  as gone.
- [Statuses and commands](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md): the four statuses, the commands, ack timeouts and Reminders.
- [Loud and Quiet](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md): which changes ring a phone, and whom they Mention.
- [Broken Destinations](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md): what happens when a messenger stops answering.

## The things Muster handles

Four words sound alike and are not the same. Muster keeps them apart:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| Snapshot | One notification from Alertmanager. It lists the current Alerts of one **Alertmanager group**. It is input, not an Alert. |
| Alertmanager group | The alerts Alertmanager notifies about together under one `groupKey`. It is Alertmanager's idea of "together", decided by the `group_by` of its route. |
| Alert | One firing problem reported by a source, identified by its full set of labels, such as one pod, one node or one domain. |
| Alert Group | The problem Muster shows people. It contains Alerts, and which ones go together is decided by a [Route and its Group key](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md), not by Alertmanager. |

Muster does not copy Alertmanager's grouping. Alertmanager's groups exist to batch notifications. An Alert Group exists
so that a person can say "I have this one". The two often look alike, but you can change either without the other.

## What an Alert Group has

Number, `#N`
:   Assigned per Organization, without gaps, when the Alert Group is created. It is what people say aloud: "I took
    #412".

Status
:   `firing`, `acknowledged`, `snoozed` or `resolved`. See [Statuses and commands](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md).

Owner
:   The user who acknowledged it. Only a user can be an Owner; a Service account cannot.

Title
:   The `alertname` that its Alerts share. When Alerts with different `alertname` values join it, the Group key values
    instead, such as `cluster=prod, namespace=payments`. It is set when the Alert Group is created and changes at most
    once, at that switch.

Summary
:   The `summary` annotation of the first of its Alerts that has one. It is set once.

Route
:   The [Route](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md) that took its Alerts. It decides the Destinations and the timers.

Severity level
:   The highest Severity level of its firing Alerts: critical, warning or info.

Urgent
:   Set when its Route is marked urgent, or when its Severity level is critical and the Organization treats critical as
    Urgent (`organization.critical_is_urgent`, on by default).

Reopen count
:   How many times Muster reopened it.

Alerts
:   One entry per fingerprint, firing first, resolved ones struck through with their reason.

Timeline
:   The ordered record of everything that happened to it.

The Alert Group page shows all of this, the Alerts with their labels and annotations, the labels they share, and the
previous Alert Groups with the same Route and Group key values. The page and the list work at phone width.

## Live updates

The list and the Alert Group page change as soon as something happens, without a reload. A mark in the header of every
page says whether these live updates reach your browser, so that on a phone at night you know whether the list in front
of you is current:

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Green filled dot, "Live" | Live updates are on. |
| Grey ring, "Connecting…" | The page has loaded and is connecting. The text shows once this has taken 5 seconds. |
| Amber half-filled dot, pulsing, "Reconnecting…" | The connection has been lost for 5 seconds, and the browser keeps trying again. |
| Red ring with a slash, "Offline" | The connection has been lost for 30 seconds, or the page has not connected within 30 seconds of loading. |

On a screen narrower than 640 pixels, such as a phone, only the dot shows, whatever the state, so that the navigation
keeps its room; each state has its own shape as well as its colour, so you can tell them apart without the colour. A
drop shorter than 5 seconds, such as a Muster replica restarting, leaves the mark as it was. Press the mark to read its
state and what it means: in every state but "Live" it says that what you see may be out of date, while reconnecting or
offline it names the time the connection was lost, and when offline it offers to reload the page. As soon as the
connection is back, the list and the page are read again, so they show everything that happened meanwhile. The mark
sends nothing to Muster.

## How Alerts join an Alert Group

When an Alert starts firing, Muster picks its [Route](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md) and reads the values of the Route's
**Group key** from the Alert's labels. Then, in this order:

1. If an **open** Alert Group of that Route has the same Group key values, the Alert joins it.
2. Otherwise, if the system resolved an Alert Group of that Route with the same values within the
   [Reopen window](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#reopening), that Alert Group reopens.
3. Otherwise a new Alert Group starts, with the next number.

An Alert that is already in an open Alert Group is not routed again: it stays there until the Alert Group is resolved,
even if you change the Route's Matchers or Group key meanwhile.

What a new Alert does to an Alert Group depends on its status, because the status says whether anybody is paying
attention:

| The Alert Group is | A new Alert joining it is |
|---|---|
| firing | a Loud event, added to the Thread in batches |
| acknowledged | a Quiet event; the acknowledgement stays, always |
| snoozed | a Quiet update of the Root message only; what accumulated is listed when the Snooze ends |

### Replacements

An exporter restarts and reports the same problem with a new `pod` label. That is a different Alert, since its labels
differ, but it is the same problem. When a new Alert differs from a firing Alert of the same Alert Group only in
[Instance labels](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#instance-labels), Muster records a **Replacement**: a Quiet event in the Timeline that names the label
that differs. The old Alert resolving is Quiet too. The Alert Group page suggests the real fix, which is to aggregate the
label away in the rule, for example with `without(pod, instance)`.

### Instance labels

Instance labels are the labels that change when the process reporting an Alert restarts. The Organization lists them in
`organization.instance_labels`; by default `pod`, `instance`, `container` and `endpoint`. See [Instance labels in
informational alerts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#instance-labels-in-informational-alerts) for when to keep them
out of your rules.

## Reopening

An Alert Group is **resolved by the system** when its last Alert resolves, whether Alertmanager said so, or the Alert
went [Gone or Stale](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md), or its Integration was deleted. A person can resolve it too.

The two ways to resolve differ in what happens when the problem returns:

| Resolved by | When an Alert with the same Route and Group key values fires again |
|---|---|
| The system | Within the **Reopen window** (`route.reopen_window`, 15 minutes by default) the same Alert Group **reopens**: same number, Reopen count plus one, and it returns to the status it had before, with the same Owner if it was acknowledged. After the window, a new Alert Group starts. |
| A person | The Reopen window does not apply. If the Alerts that were still firing are still reported when the **Grace period** (`route.grace_period`, 15 minutes by default) ends, they are grouped again as if they had just fired. Within the Grace period, a new firing starts a new Alert Group at once. |

A reopen is keyed by the Route and the Group key values, not by one Alert: any Alert with the same values brings the
Alert Group back, whether it is one of its own Alerts or a new one. How loud a reopen is depends on where it returns:
Loud into firing, Loud into acknowledged but Mentioning only the Owner, Quiet into snoozed.

A person who resolved the wrong Alert Group presses **Unresolve** in the web UI or the API. Unresolve is not offered in
messengers, and it works only on an Alert Group that a person resolved, not on one that reopens by itself.

The reason is always visible. A resolution by the system carries the reason, such as "Alertmanager no longer reports this
alert", and so does every other automatic change; the page, the Timeline and the message show it.

## Where an Alert Group shows up

A Route lists the Destinations that receive its Alert Groups. For each Alert Group and each of its Destinations, Muster
keeps one **Root message** and brings it to the latest state each time something changes. Replies, such as new Alerts
joining or a Reminder, go to the message's **Thread**. See [Loud and Quiet](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md) for which changes are new
messages and which are edits.

An Alert Group whose Route has no Destination, as with the Default route in the [Quick start](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/quick-start.md), exists
only in Muster. Its page, the list, the statistics and the Timeline still work.

## The Timeline

The Timeline of an Alert Group shows, in order: Alerts added, resolved, replaced and continued; status changes with the
actor and the Transport; Reopens; Notes; Takeovers; ack timeout notices, Reminders and their answers; use of the
Fallback template; delivery events such as a Publication, a possible duplicate or a delivery that was Not delivered;
moves to the Default route; and the periods when Muster itself was down. Each entry that records something Muster might
tell people also shows whether it was Loud and whom it Mentioned.

You can filter the Timeline by kind and read it oldest first or newest first. Notes belong to it: Responders and Admins
can add one, up to 4,000 characters (`alert_group.note_max_length`).

## Changing a Route does not change an Alert Group

Edits of a Route's settings apply at once, also to its open Alert Groups, whose messages are updated. They never change
an Alert Group's status. A new Group key or new Matchers apply only to Alerts that start firing afterwards.

A Route that still has open Alert Groups cannot be deleted. Muster refuses and offers to move them to the Default
route. A moved Alert Group keeps its Group key values, takes no new Alerts, and never reopens; it stays open until its
Alerts resolve or a person resolves it.

## How long Alert Groups are kept

`retention.alert_details`
:   kept for: 90 days

    Alerts in Alert Groups, Timeline entries, delivery events.

`retention.alert_group_summaries`
:   kept for: 2 years

    The summary row of an Alert Group: number, title, summary, times, Route, status, and its Notes.

After the details are removed, search still finds the Alert Group by its title and number, and its page shows the
summary with the notice that the Alerts and the Timeline were removed. The list shows Alert Groups whose lifetime
overlaps the chosen time range, 7 days by default (`alert_group.list_range`), so an Alert Group that has been firing for
weeks is always in the default view. Searching by number ignores the range.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md -->
# Routes and Group keys

A **Route** decides what happens to an Alert after Muster has read it: which Alert Group it joins, who is told, and how
the Alert Group is handled afterwards. A **Group key** decides which Alerts share an Alert Group. Together they are the
two settings that shape what your team sees.

Do not confuse a Route with an **Alertmanager route**. An Alertmanager route is a rule inside Alertmanager that picks a
receiver and a repeat interval. A Route of Muster is evaluated after the Alert has arrived, on the labels of the Alert.

## How an Alert is routed

1. The Alert arrives in a [Snapshot](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md) of an Integration.
2. The Integration's **Static labels** are added to it. If the Alert already has a label of that name, its own value
   wins, and Muster warns about the label.
3. Muster walks the Routes in list order. The first Route whose Matchers all match takes the Alert.
4. The Route's Group key says which Alert Group the Alert goes to. See [Alert Groups](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#how-alerts-join-an-alert-group).

Only an Alert that starts firing is routed. An Alert that already lives in an open Alert Group stays in it.

## Routes

A Route has:

- a **name**, unique in the Organization, and a description;
- **Matchers**, which pick the Alerts;
- a **position** in the list;
- an **urgent** mark;
- a **Group key**;
- the **Destinations** that receive its Alert Groups;
- policy fields for how its Alert Groups are handled: the Reopen window and the Grace period, whether a rise to Urgent
  removes an acknowledgement, the Snooze durations, the Thread batching window and the Storm threshold, the templates
  and the language, and the ack timeout, the Reminders and auto-unacknowledge.

### Matchers

A Matcher is a condition on one label, written as in Alertmanager: `=`, `!=`, `=~` and `!~`, where the last two take an
RE2 regular expression. The Matchers of a Route are all required: they combine with AND. The Route editor builds them
from fields; the API takes the same structure; an invalid expression is refused with a pointer to the field.

`team="payments"` and `severity="critical"`
:   Takes Alerts of the payments team that are critical.

`namespace=~"prod-.*"`
:   Takes Alerts in any namespace that starts with `prod-`.

`alertname!="Watchdog"`
:   Takes everything except the Watchdog.

A missing label counts as an empty value. So `team!="payments"` also matches an Alert that has no `team` label.

### Order, and the Default route

Routes are evaluated in list order, and the first Route that matches takes the Alert. Put the narrow Routes first and
the broad ones after them. Drag the Routes on the Routes page to reorder them.

The **Default route** is always last. It has no Matchers, cannot be deleted or moved, and takes every Alert that no other
Route took. A small installation may keep only the Default route. A Route with no Destinations is fine too: its Alert
Groups exist in Muster and in no messenger.

Edits to Routes use optimistic locking: if somebody changed the Routes while you were editing, your save is refused and
you reload.

### Route profiles

When you create a Route, you choose a **Route profile**. A profile only fills in the settings; it is not stored, and you
can change every field afterwards. There are two:

Ack timeout (`route.ack_timeout`)
:   On-call: on; first notice after 15 minutes · Informational: off

Reminders (`route.reminders`)
:   On-call: on; first after 4 hours · Informational: off

Snooze durations (`route.snooze_durations`)
:   On-call: 1 h, 4 h, 24 h · Informational: 1 d, 3 d, 7 d

Group key (`route.group_key`)
:   On-call: `alertname`, `severity`, `cluster` · Informational: the same

Reopen window and Grace period
:   On-call: 15 minutes each · Informational: the same

Choose **Informational** for alerts nobody needs to act on at once, such as a certificate that expires in a month: no
notices, no Reminders, and long Snooze durations. Choose **On-call** for the rest. See [Statuses and
commands](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#ack-timeouts-reminders-and-auto-unacknowledge) for what the timers do.

### Urgent

An Alert Group is **Urgent** when its Route is marked urgent, or when its Severity level is critical and the Organization
has `organization.critical_is_urgent` on (the default). An Urgent Alert Group is posted first when many arrive at once,
and a rise to Urgent can end a Snooze or remove an acknowledgement.

By default the `severity` label maps to a Severity level: `critical` is critical, `warning` is warning, `info` and
`none` are info, any other value counts as warning and is shown as received, and an Alert without the label counts as
info. The Organization can change the label and the mapping.

## Group keys

The **Group key** of a Route is a list of label names. Alerts of the Route that have the same values for all of those
labels go to the same Alert Group. A label that an Alert lacks counts as an empty value, so Alerts that all lack
`cluster` group together.

The default Group key is `alertname`, `severity` and `cluster`. Take these four Alerts, all taken by one Route:

| Alert | `alertname` | `severity` | `cluster` | `namespace` | `pod` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `KubePodCrashLooping` | `warning` | `prod` | `payments` | `api-1` |
| 2 | `KubePodCrashLooping` | `warning` | `prod` | `payments` | `api-2` |
| 3 | `KubePodCrashLooping` | `warning` | `prod` | `search` | `web-1` |
| 4 | `KubePodCrashLooping` | `warning` | `staging` | `payments` | `api-1` |

| Group key | Alert Groups | Which Alerts |
|---|---|---|
| `alertname`, `severity`, `cluster` (default) | 2 | 1, 2 and 3 in one; 4 in another |
| `alertname`, `cluster`, `namespace` | 3 | 1 and 2; 3; 4 |
| `alertname`, `cluster`, `namespace`, `pod` | 4 | one Alert Group per pod |
| `alertname` | 1 | all four |

There is no best key. A coarse key gives few Alert Groups that stay open longer, and a person takes the whole problem
with one Acknowledge. A fine key gives more Alert Groups and a clearer ownership of each. Pick the labels that tell
"who should look at this" apart. A good start is the labels your teams split on: the alert name, the cluster and the
namespace or the service.

### Preview before you save

The Group key editor previews what a key would do. It reads the Stored Snapshots of the chosen period (24 hours by
default, at most the retention of Stored Snapshots; `routing.group_key_preview_period`) and shows how many Alert Groups
the current and the proposed key would produce, with the 5 largest as examples (`routing.group_key_preview_examples`).
It covers the Alerts that the Route would take
at its place in the current order, each Alert once, and it works for a Route you are still creating. Use it before every
change of a key.

### Do not put Instance labels in the key

**Instance labels** change when the process that reports an Alert restarts, such as `pod` and `instance`. If one is in the
Group key, every restart of a pod starts an Alert Group of its own and the old one stays open. Keep `pod` and `instance`
out of the key unless one Alert Group per pod is what you want. When it is, restarts cause no trouble, since the Alert Group
for a pod fires and resolves with that pod. Otherwise leave the labels out of the key, so that the restarted pod's
Alert is recognised as a **Replacement** inside the same Alert Group. See [Alert Groups](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#replacements)
and [Instance labels in informational alerts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#instance-labels-in-informational-alerts).

### Static labels

**Static labels** belong to an Integration, not to the Route. Muster adds them to every Alert of the Integration before it
routes it, so the Matchers and the Group key can use them like labels the rules set. Their usual job is to name what
the Alertmanager cluster knows and the rules do not, such as `cluster=prod-eu`. That is why the default Group key can
include `cluster`: set it as a Static label on each Integration, and Alert Groups of different clusters stay apart even
when the alerting rules never mention the cluster. See [Static
labels](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#static-labels).

## Examples

**Only the Default route.** Every Alert goes to one Route, grouped by `alertname`, `severity` and `cluster`. Add one
Destination to the Default route and everything reaches one place. This is the setup of the [Quick start](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/quick-start.md)
plus a messenger.

**Pages for payments.** Create the Route `payments-critical` with the Matchers `team="payments"` and
`severity="critical"`, the On-call profile, the urgent mark on, and a Destination that is the payments team's channel.
Put it above the Default route. Critical alerts of the payments team reach their channel and are Urgent. Their other
alerts fall through to the Default route.

**Certificates.** Create the Route `certificates` with the Matcher `alertname=~"Cert.*"`, the Informational profile and a
Destination for the platform channel. These Alert Groups send no ack timeout notices and no Reminders, and they offer
Snooze for a day, three days or a week.

**Muster's own alerts.** The Internal alerts, such as `MusterDestinationBroken`, are Alerts of the built-in "Muster"
Integration and are routed by Routes like any other. Route them to a Destination of another kind than the one that
failed. The Routes page offers a Route for `alertname=~"Muster.*"` once you have a Destination, and a Route for
`MusterHeartbeatLost` when an Integration has a [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md). See the [Internal
alerts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/internal-alerts.md).

## What changes when you edit a Route

- Settings, such as the timers, the templates and the Snooze durations, apply at once, also to open Alert Groups, whose
  messages are brought up to date.
- A new Group key or new Matchers apply to Alerts that start firing afterwards. A fingerprint already in an open Alert
  Group stays there until that Alert Group is resolved.
- No edit changes the status of any Alert Group.
- Adding a Destination to a Route gives it the Route's open Alert Groups, Quietly. Removing one gives each open Root
  message one last edit that says it is no longer updated and links to Muster.
- Deleting a Route that has open Alert Groups is refused. You can move them to the Default route first.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md -->
# Snapshot semantics

Alertmanager does not tell Muster "this alert started" and "this alert stopped" as separate events. It sends a
**Snapshot**: the full state of one Alertmanager group at the moment of the notification, listing every alert it holds.
Grafana's built-in Alertmanager sends Snapshots too, through a webhook contact point.
Muster works out what changed by comparing Snapshots. This page explains the rules, and why an alert can be **Gone** or
**Stale** without anybody sending a "resolved".

You only need this page to understand why Muster resolved something, or why it did not. The settings that matter are on
[Connect Alertmanager](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md), in particular its
[Repeat intervals](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#repeat-intervals), and on
[Connect Grafana](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md).

## From a Snapshot to a message

Receiving is store-first. Muster checks the Integration token and the size, stores the Snapshot exactly as received, and
answers `202`. A worker then processes it, on any replica, and everything that follows is a chain of small steps:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  am["Alertmanager or Grafana"] -- "Snapshot" --> ingest["Ingest"]
  ingest --> stored[("Stored Snapshot")]
  stored --> processing["Processing"]
  processing -- "Alert changes" --> routing["Routing"]
  routing -- "Route" --> groups["Alert Group"]
  groups -- "lifecycle event" --> desired["Desired state"]
  desired --> worker["Delivery worker"]
  worker --> root["Root message"]
```

1. **Ingest** stores the Snapshot as a **Stored Snapshot** and wakes a worker. It is kept for
   `retention.stored_snapshots` (14 days) for debugging, previews and replay.
2. **Processing** splits the Snapshot into Alerts by fingerprint, adds the Integration's Static labels, and applies the
   rules below. It emits Alert changes: a new firing, a resolution with its reason, a Continuation, a change of
   annotations. It processes the Snapshots of an Alertmanager group in the order they arrived.
3. **Routing** gives each newly firing Alert its Route and Severity level.
4. The **Alert Group** takes the Alert: it joins an open one, reopens a resolved one, or starts a new one. Every change
   records a lifecycle event in the Timeline.
5. The lifecycle event changes the **Desired state** of the Alert Group's message in each of its Destinations: what the
   Root message should look like right now.
6. The **delivery worker** brings the actual message to the Desired state with one call, and the **Root message** in the
   messenger shows it. See [Loud and Quiet](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md) for when that is an edit and when a new message.

Processing writes one log line per Snapshot, never one per Alert.

## One Alertmanager group, one stream of Snapshots

An Alertmanager group is the set of alerts that Alertmanager notifies about together under one `groupKey`. The
Snapshots of one group form a stream, and Muster compares each with the ones before it. Alertmanager sends a Snapshot
again each time the group changes and each time the route's `repeat_interval` elapses, and Muster learns from the gaps.

Two things about Snapshots matter in practice:

- **Copies from an HA pair are harmless.** Two Alertmanagers in a pair send their own copy, 0 to 15 seconds apart,
  sometimes one of them incomplete. Muster processes an Alert once for the same fingerprint, status and `startsAt`, so a
  duplicate changes nothing. Snapshots of one group that arrive within the Integration's **duplicate window**
  (`integration.duplicate_window`, 45 seconds) count as one, and an Alert listed in either of them counts as listed.
- **A Snapshot's status is the group's, an Alert's status is its own.** A Snapshot with `status: firing` can list alerts
  that are resolved, and each alert's own status decides for it.

## Resolved

The normal way an Alert ends is that Alertmanager lists it as `resolved`. Muster resolves it at once, with the reason
that Alertmanager resolved it, in the latest Alert Group where that fingerprint is still firing.

- A `resolved` for an Alert that is already resolved, or for an earlier firing of it, changes nothing. Prometheus re-sends
  a resolved alert for about 15 minutes, so the same `resolved` arrives several times.
- A `resolved` with an older `startsAt` than the Alert's current one resolves the current firing when its `endsAt` is
  later than the current `startsAt`: the two firings overlap. The replicas of a Grafana HA pair evaluate the rules each
  on its own, so their copies of one alert can carry different `startsAt`, and the resolve of either replica ends the
  Alert. Without an `endsAt`, or with one not later than the current `startsAt`, it is a resolve of an earlier firing.
  Alertmanager merges overlapping firings of one alert, so with one rule evaluator a resolve it sends of an earlier
  firing ends before the next one starts. With an HA pair of rule evaluators, such as two Prometheus replicas, it can
  send one that ends later, and Muster resolves the Alert, as it would with the `startsAt` that Alertmanager merged.
- A `resolved` for a fingerprint that fires nowhere is dropped, and counted.
- A Snapshot whose status is `resolved`, sent when all the alerts of its group resolved, resolves **every Alert of that
  group** that still fires, also the ones it does not list. After a restart of both Alertmanagers of a pair, such a
  Snapshot can list only some of them and the others are never sent. A truncated Snapshot from Grafana is the
  exception; see [Truncation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md#truncation).

## Gone

Sometimes Alertmanager stops listing an alert without saying that it resolved. The rule evaluator may have stopped, an
alert may have been inhibited, or the route may have changed. Muster notices that the Alert is **Gone**:

> An Alert is Gone in an Alertmanager group when it has been missing from **at least two consecutive Snapshots** of that
> group, over **at least `processing.gone_min_absence`** (5 minutes), counted from the first Snapshot that missed it to
> the latest one.

A Snapshot that lists it ends the count. Both conditions are needed, for good reasons. A restarted Alertmanager starts
with an empty memory, and its first Snapshots can leave out a firing alert twice, a minute apart, because Prometheus
re-sends firing alerts only every 2 minutes. The minimum absence covers that. A restarted instance of an HA pair is
covered by the duplicate window, because the other instance sends the full Snapshot 15 seconds later.

| Snapshots of one group | Result |
|---|---|
| Alert A missing at T and T+60 s, listed at T+120 s | A stays firing; the count restarts |
| Alert A missing at T, T+60 s and T+6 min | A is Gone at T+6 min |
| Alert A missing at T only | A stays firing; one Snapshot never counts |

An Alert that appears in several Alertmanager groups is resolved by absence only when it is Gone (or Stale) in **every**
one of them.

## Stale

If the whole group sends nothing at all, there is no Snapshot to miss the Alert from. This happens when the group is
silenced, inhibited or muted as a whole in Alertmanager. Muster calls an Alert **Stale** when it has heard nothing about
it for too long:

> An Alert goes Stale when its Alertmanager group has sent no Snapshot for `stale_after`, which is
> `processing.stale_after_factor` (3) times the repeat interval that Muster has learned for the group's Alertmanager
> route.

Muster learns the interval from the gaps between Snapshots whose `notification_reason` is `repeat interval elapsed` or,
from senders without that field such as Grafana, between identical Snapshots, and uses the median of the last 9 gaps (`processing.repeat_samples`).
Until it has learned an interval, `stale_after` is `processing.stale_after_unlearned`, 25 hours. Alertmanager sends a
repeat on the first `group_interval` tick after `repeat_interval` has elapsed, so the gaps are about `repeat_interval` +
`group_interval`. With a 10-minute `repeat_interval` and Alertmanager's default `group_interval` of 5 minutes, Muster
learns an interval of about 15 minutes, and a silenced group's Alerts go Stale after about 45 minutes. With a daily
interval it takes more than three days, which is why the Integration page warns about an interval longer than
`processing.long_repeat_warning` (1 hour). See [Repeat intervals](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#repeat-intervals).

Gone and Stale both resolve the Alert with the reason "Alertmanager no longer reports this alert — it resolved without
notice, was silenced or inhibited in Alertmanager, or the Alertmanager routing changed". If a silenced alert's mute
ends within about 14 minutes, Alertmanager still reports it as resolved, so it resolves normally; after that it only
goes Stale.

## The Heartbeat

Stale resolution has a risk: if the path from Alertmanager to Muster breaks, Muster hears nothing, and every Alert would
go Stale, although they may still fire. The [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md) removes the risk. It is a regular
signal that proves the path works.

- **Stale applies only while the Integration's Heartbeat is live.** An Integration without a Heartbeat, or still waiting
  for the first signal, never resolves an Alert as Stale. Gone still works.
- While the Heartbeat is **lost** (no signal within `integration.heartbeat_timeout`, 5 minutes), the time does not count
  towards `stale_after`. From the last signal before the loss until the signal returns, nothing goes Stale. Muster's own
  downtime does not count either, beyond the timeout.
- The Integration shows "No contact with Alertmanager since HH:MM", and Muster raises the Internal alert
  `MusterHeartbeatLost`.

So with a live Heartbeat and a learned 5-minute interval, an Alert whose group last arrived at T goes Stale at T+15
minutes. If the last Heartbeat signal also came at T, the Heartbeat was lost at T+5 minutes, and the signal returned at
T+10 minutes, the Alert goes Stale at T+25 minutes: the 10 minutes from the last signal until its return did not count.

## Truncation

An Alertmanager webhook configuration with `max_alerts` above 0, like Grafana's webhook contact point with Max alerts
above 0, keeps only the first alerts of a group in each notification, and counts the rest in `truncatedAlerts`. A
truncated Snapshot lists only part of the group, so it can never be evidence that an Alert is missing.

- Muster does **not** count a truncated Snapshot as absence. While Snapshots of the group keep arriving truncated, the
  unlisted Alerts stay alive, which can keep an Alert open that has resolved in reality.
- Muster raises the Internal alert `MusterSnapshotTruncated` for the Integration while any group is truncated, and
  resolves it when none is left. The Integration page shows a warning too.
- Grafana computes the status of a Snapshot from the alerts it lists, not from the whole group, so a truncated
  Snapshot from Grafana can say `resolved` while alerts it left out still fire. Muster recognises a Snapshot from
  Grafana by its top-level `orgId`, which Alertmanager never sends. A truncated one with `status: resolved` resolves
  only the Alerts it lists as resolved, never its whole group.
- The fix is `max_alerts: 0` on the Alertmanager receiver, or Max alerts 0, the default, on Grafana's webhook contact
  point. See [Send every alert of the group](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md#send-every-alert-of-the-group),
  [Connect Grafana](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/grafana.md#create-a-webhook-contact-point) and the
  [runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterSnapshotTruncated.md).

## Continuation

A Prometheus restart whose first evaluation falls exactly on the alerts' `endsAt` can make Alertmanager send them again
with a new `startsAt` and no `resolved` in between. A longer stop gives a `resolved` and a new firing. That first case
is a **Continuation**: the Alert stays the same, its start time is updated, and nothing is Loud and nothing reopens.
Once an Alert has resolved by any route, the next firing of the same fingerprint is a new firing.

## Why an Alert resolved

Every Alert resolved by Muster carries one of four reasons, which the Integration's Alerts view shows and the metric
`muster_alerts_resolved_total` counts:

`resolved`
:   Alertmanager sent `resolved`, for the Alert or for its whole group.

`gone`
:   Missing from at least two consecutive Snapshots for the minimum absence.

`stale`
:   Its group sent nothing for three learned repeat intervals, with a live Heartbeat.

`integration_deleted`
:   Its Integration was deleted.

When the last Alert of an Alert Group resolves, the Alert Group is resolved by the system with the reason of the last
one. See [Alert Groups](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#reopening) for what happens if the problem returns. If processing ever misbehaves,
`muster ingest replay` reprocesses Stored Snapshots, and because processing is idempotent it changes nothing that was
already right.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md -->
# Loud and Quiet

Every change to an Alert Group is either **Loud** or **Quiet**. A Loud change should make people's devices ring. A Quiet
change should only update what they see when they look. Muster fixes the loudness of every change; you decide only whom
a Loud change **Mentions**.

The rule behind it is simple, and it is the same in Mattermost, Slack and Telegram: **an edit never notifies anybody.**
Editing a message, even to add a Mention, does not ring a phone. So a Loud change is always a **new message**, a new
Root message or a reply in the Thread, and a Quiet change is an edit of the Root message or a new message without a
Mention.

## Which changes are Loud

A new Alert Group starts
:   Loud, as a new Root message · mentions: the Destination's `new_alert_group` setting

New Alerts join a **firing** Alert Group
:   Loud, as a Thread reply; batched · mentions: `new_alerts`

New Alerts join an acknowledged or snoozed Alert Group
:   Quiet · mentions: nobody

A Reopen into firing
:   Loud · mentions: `reopen`

A Reopen into acknowledged
:   Loud · mentions: the Owner only

A Reopen into snoozed
:   Quiet · mentions: nobody

A Snooze ends while Alerts still fire
:   Loud, listing what accumulated · mentions: `snooze_ended`

A rise to Urgent that ends a Snooze or removes an acknowledgement
:   Loud, with the reason · mentions: the Owner it removed, and `rise_to_urgent`

A rise in Severity level that changes nothing else
:   Quiet · mentions: nobody

A Takeover
:   Loud · mentions: the previous Owner

An ack timeout notice
:   Loud · mentions: `ack_timeout`

A Reminder
:   Loud · mentions: the Owner

Auto-unacknowledge
:   Loud, with the reason · mentions: the Owner it removed

The Owner is disabled or deleted
:   Loud · mentions: nobody

Several notices missed during downtime
:   Loud, as one reply · mentions: as the notices it stands for

Acknowledge, Unacknowledge, Snooze, Unsnooze, Resolve, Unresolve
:   Quiet · mentions: nobody

An Alert resolves, is replaced or continues, or its annotations change
:   Quiet · mentions: nobody

The system resolves the Alert Group
:   Quiet, with a Thread reply that gives the reason · mentions: nobody

A Note
:   Quiet, and not sent to messengers · mentions: nobody

The pattern: Muster rings when something needs a human who may not be looking, such as a new problem, one that returned,
one that nobody took, or one that someone took and went quiet. It does not ring for what a person just did, because that
person is looking. The Takeover is the only result of a person's command that is Loud, because the previous Owner has
just lost the Alert Group.

Delivery adds a few cases of its own:

| Delivery event | Loud or Quiet |
|---|---|
| A Destination added to a Route receives its open Alert Groups | Quiet |
| A Destination recovers from [Broken](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md): an Alert Group still firing is published | Loud |
| The same recovery, for an Alert Group that is not firing, or an edit of a message already there | Quiet |
| A message published late, after the Alert Group already resolved | Quiet, with a note |
| A Root message posted again because it was deleted | Quiet, with a note |
| A Storm summary, when it first appears | Loud |
| A Storm summary's updates, and the Alert Groups posted after the Storm | Quiet |

You cannot change the loudness of an event. You can change whom it Mentions.

## What Loud means in each Destination

Mattermost
:   A Loud change is a new post, with its Mentions in the text of the post.

    A Quiet change is an edit, or a new post without a Mention.

Slack
:   A Loud change is a new message, a Root message or a reply in the Thread, with its Mentions.

    A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message without a Mention.

Telegram
:   A Loud change is a new message, in the channel for a Root message and in the discussion group for a Thread reply.

    A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message sent with `disable_notification`.

Bridge
:   A Loud change is a new message that the bridge posts with `notify` on, with its Mentions.

    A Quiet change is an edit, or a new message that the bridge posts without a notification where it declares
    `quiet_messages`.

Outgoing webhook
:   A Loud change is an event with `notify` true (events mode), or `.Notify` true in a template (template mode).

    A Quiet change is `notify` false.

A few details:

- **Mattermost.** A reply in a Thread notifies the Thread's followers by their own settings, and a Mention makes the
  person a follower. So Quiet means "without a Mention", not "nobody is notified". Mentions are in the text of the
  post and never in the attachment, because a Mention in an attachment notifies with an empty notification. See [Who
  gets notified](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/mattermost.md#who-gets-notified).
- **Slack.** Slack cannot send a message without a notification: whom a new message notifies depends on each member's
  settings for the channel and the Thread. So Quiet means "without a Mention", not "nobody is notified". An edit carries
  no Mention, so it drops the Mentions of the message it edits. See [Who gets
  notified](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md#who-gets-notified).
- **Telegram.** `disable_notification` silences the sound but does not remove the push. Only members of the channel's
  discussion group get Thread replies, and the automatic copy of every Root message rings them, even for a Quiet one.
  Tell the people on call to join the group and mute the channel itself. See [Known limitation: Quiet Root messages ring
  the group](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/telegram.md#known-limitation-quiet-root-messages-ring-the-group).
- **Bridge.** Whether the bridge can post without a notification depends on the bridge. A bridge that does not declare
  `quiet_messages` posts a Quiet message as an ordinary one, without Mentions.
- **Outgoing webhook.** Muster rings nothing itself. In events mode every event is sent, Quiet ones too, with `notify`
  telling what a person-facing system should do with it. Your receiver decides, for example, to call a phone only when
  `notify` is true. See [events mode](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/events.md#event-names) and [Recipes](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/recipes.md).

## Mentions

A **Mention** is a deliberate @-reference that Muster adds to a message so that a person is notified. Muster adds a
Mention only where this page says it does. Alert data never mention anyone: an `@` in a label or an annotation is
neutralized with a zero-width space, so `@channel` in a label notifies nobody.

### Whom a Loud change Mentions

Each Destination has a **Mention setting** for each of six kinds of Loud change:

- `new_alert_group`, `new_alerts`, `reopen`, `ack_timeout`, `snooze_ended` and `rise_to_urgent`.

For each, the Destination chooses **nobody** (the default for all six), **everyone in the chat**, **chosen Muster users**,
or **messenger groups**. What a Destination type offers:

| Destination | Nobody | Everyone in the chat | Chosen users | Messenger groups |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mattermost | yes | `@channel`, `@all` or `@here` | yes | Mattermost group names |
| Slack | yes | `@channel` or `@here` | yes | no |
| Telegram | yes | no | yes | no |
| Bridge | yes | no | yes | no |
| Outgoing webhook | yes | yes, as data | yes, as data | yes, as data |

Some Mentions are not a setting. A **Reminder** and an auto-unacknowledge always Mention the Owner, a **Takeover**
Mentions the previous Owner, and a Reopen into acknowledged Mentions only the Owner.

### Account links

A Mention of a user needs an **Account link**: the tie between a Muster user and their account in the messenger. The
people who are Mentioned, and the Owner above all, link their accounts from their profile; see [Link your messenger
accounts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md). Muster renders a Mention in the messenger's own form:

- Mattermost: `@username`;
- Slack: a Mention of the person's Slack account;
- Telegram: a link to the person, whose text is the display name;
- Bridge: a marker that a bridge with `native_mentions` renders as the messenger's mention and any other bridge as the
  person's name.

**A user without an Account link is named by their display name as plain text, which notifies nobody.** So choosing a
user for a Mention setting, or being an Owner, rings a phone only once that person has linked their account. The footer
of a Root message names a person by their messenger username without `@`, which does not notify them either.

For an outgoing webhook, Muster does not know the receiver's markup, so the Mention is data: the event's `mentions`
list, and `.Mentions` in a template, with the target's type, id, name and login. Your receiver or your template turns
it into whatever the receiving system understands.

## Storm summaries

When many Alert Groups start at once, one Route can flood a Destination. A **Storm** is a Route creating more new Alert
Groups in one minute than its Storm threshold (`route.storm_threshold`, 20 by default). Then each of the Route's
Destinations gets one **Storm summary** instead of a message per Alert Group:

- The summary is Loud only when it first appears, and Mentions as a new Alert Group does (`new_alert_group`).
- **Urgent** Alert Groups are still posted on their own, first.
- Its updates and its final state are Quiet. When the rate has stayed below the threshold for 5 minutes
  (`delivery.storm_calm_period`), the summary shows its final state, and the Alert Groups that are still open are
  posted gradually and Quietly. Those that already resolved are not posted.
- Messengers and the template mode of outgoing webhooks follow Storms. The events mode does not: it receives every event.

## Why the rule is fixed

A rule of thumb for on-call: the phones should ring for problems that need a human, and nothing else. Because an edit is
always silent, a person can acknowledge, snooze and resolve all day, and the message changes under their eyes without a
sound; and because the loudness of every change is fixed, a team never has to wonder whether a change will ring. The
Mention settings are the one place to tune who rings.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md -->
# Statuses and commands

An Alert Group is always in one of four statuses, and only a few things move it from one to another. Some are
**Commands** that a person gives, from the web UI, the API, a button in a messenger, or a Text command in a Thread. The
others are transitions that Muster makes on its own, always with a reason you can read.

## The four statuses

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Firing** | The Alert Group has a live problem and nobody has taken it. |
| **Acknowledged** | A person has taken it and is handling it. That person is its **Owner**. |
| **Snoozed** | It is set aside until a chosen time, or with no end. Muster stays quiet about it meanwhile. |
| **Resolved** | It is closed, by a person or by Muster because its Alerts are gone. |

New Alerts that join an open Alert Group change its status only through a rise to Urgent, and edits of a Route never
change a status. Only the transitions below do.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Resolved by the system" as ResolvedBySystem
    state "Resolved by a user" as ResolvedByUser

    [*] --> Firing : created
    Firing --> Acknowledged : Acknowledge
    Snoozed --> Acknowledged : Acknowledge
    Acknowledged --> Acknowledged : Takeover
    Acknowledged --> Firing : Unacknowledge
```
