```mermaid
    Acknowledged --> Firing : auto-unacknowledge (system)
    Acknowledged --> Firing : rise to Urgent (system)
    Firing --> Snoozed : Snooze
    Acknowledged --> Snoozed : Snooze
    Snoozed --> Snoozed : Snooze with a new end
    Snoozed --> Firing : Unsnooze
    Snoozed --> Firing : Snooze ends (system)
    Snoozed --> Firing : rise to Urgent (system)
    Firing --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Acknowledged --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Snoozed --> ResolvedByUser : Resolve
    Firing --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    Acknowledged --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    Snoozed --> ResolvedBySystem : all Alerts resolved (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Firing : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Acknowledged : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedBySystem --> Snoozed : Reopen (system)
    ResolvedByUser --> Firing : Unresolve
    ResolvedBySystem --> [*] : Reopen window ends
    ResolvedByUser --> [*] : Grace period ends
```

Resolved appears twice because the two ways back differ. After the system resolved an Alert Group, it **reopens** by
itself if the problem returns within the Reopen window. After a person resolved it, nothing reopens it; the person can
**Unresolve** it, or Muster starts a new Alert Group if the Alerts still fire after the Grace period. See
[Reopening](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/alert-groups.md#reopening).

The ack timeout runs only while an Alert Group is Firing, and an Alert Group is **Unclaimed** after its last notice. See
[Ack timeouts, Reminders and auto-unacknowledge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#ack-timeouts-reminders-and-auto-unacknowledge).

### Transitions Muster makes on its own

Each carries its reason, which you see on the Alert Group page, in its Timeline and, in a messenger, in the Root
message or a Thread reply.

Open → Resolved
:   reason you see: the reason of the last Alert

    The last Alert resolved: Alertmanager sent `resolved`, or the Alert went [Gone or Stale](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/snapshot-semantics.md), or
    its Integration was deleted. This also ends a Snooze.

Resolved by the system → previous status
:   reason you see: the Reopen, with the Reopen count

    An Alert with the same Route and Group key values fires within the Reopen window.

Snoozed → Firing
:   reason you see: the Snooze ended

    The Snooze ends while Alerts still fire. It has no Owner, and the message lists what accumulated.

Snoozed or Acknowledged → Firing
:   reason you see: the rise to Urgent

    A rise in Severity level makes the Alert Group Urgent. It ends a Snooze, unless the Snooze was set while the Alert
    Group was already Urgent, and removes an acknowledgement when the Route has `route.urgent_rise_removes_ack` on (the
    default).

Acknowledged → Firing
:   reason you see: "No answer to the last two Reminders"

    The Route's auto-unacknowledge removes the acknowledgement of an Owner who stopped answering.

Acknowledged → Firing
:   reason you see: "The owner was disabled" or "The owner was deleted"

    The Owner was disabled or deleted.

## Commands

| Command | Allowed from | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Acknowledge** | Firing, Snoozed | The caller becomes the Owner. It ends a Snooze. By the current Owner it changes nothing. By another user it is a **Takeover**. |
| **Unacknowledge** | Acknowledged | The Alert Group is Firing again, without an Owner, and the ack timeout starts over. Any user who may acknowledge can do it, not only the Owner. |
| **Resolve** | Firing, Acknowledged, Snoozed | The Alert Group is Resolved by the person. A Note can come with it. |
| **Unresolve** | Resolved by a person | The Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner. Web UI and API only. |
| **Snooze** | Firing, Acknowledged, Snoozed | The Alert Group is Snoozed until a time in the future, until a [Snooze preset](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#snooze-presets), or with no end. A Snooze with a new end changes the end. |
| **Unsnooze** | Snoozed | The Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner, and the ack timeout starts over. |
| **Add Note** | any | A Note appears in the Timeline with its author. Web UI and API only. |
| **Still on it** | Acknowledged, while a Reminder waits | The Owner answers the Reminder. See below. |

Details:

- **Takeover.** Acknowledging an Alert Group that somebody else owns moves it to you, without asking. The previous Owner
  is Mentioned in a Loud Thread reply, and your Reminders start from zero. The web UI says "Take over from {Owner}" on the
  button.
- **Snooze.** The web UI and the API accept any future time, a [Snooze preset](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#snooze-presets), or no end. The API
  makes you say which: a request names exactly one of `until`, `no_end` and `preset`. A Snooze with no end asks you to
  confirm "This Alert Group stays snoozed until someone unsnoozes it".
  Messengers offer the Route's **Snooze durations** as separate buttons or a menu (`route.snooze_durations`: 1 hour,
  4 hours and 24 hours on an On-call Route, 1 day, 3 days and 7 days on an Informational Route), and after them the
  two Snooze presets; see [In messengers](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#in-messengers).
- **Unresolve** is refused when the system resolved the Alert Group ("it reopens by itself when an alert returns"),
  when its Route was deleted, when a newer open Alert Group with the same key exists, and when all its Alerts have
  already resolved.
- **Notes** are up to 4,000 characters (`alert_group.note_max_length`).
- **Bulk commands.** In the list, select up to 100 Alert Groups (`alert_group.bulk_max`) and run Acknowledge, Resolve,
  Snooze or Unsnooze on all of them. Each goes through the rules on its own and the result lists the outcome per Alert
  Group. One refusal never stops the others. A bulk Acknowledge skips an Alert Group that another user owns ("skipped:
  owned by {Owner}"), so it never takes over by accident.
- **Refusals** carry a stable code and a message, such as "already resolved", "not acknowledged" or "not permitted". The
  API answers `409` for a precondition and `403` for a permission.
- Commands on one Alert Group are serialized. Two people acknowledging at the same moment leave the later one as Owner and
  one Takeover in the Timeline.

Every command is a Quiet event except the Takeover. See [Loud and Quiet](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/loud-and-quiet.md).

### Snooze presets

A **Snooze preset** ends a Snooze at the start of the working day instead of after a duration. Muster turns it into an
end when the command runs:

Until tomorrow 09:00
:   API value: `tomorrow` · ends at: the next start of the working day

Until Monday 09:00
:   API value: `week_start` · ends at: the next start of the working day on the first day of the week

"Next" is strictly after now. With the working day starting at 09:00:

- At 02:00, "Until tomorrow 09:00" ends at 09:00 the same day. The night belongs to the day before it, so "tomorrow"
  is the morning about to come, seven hours away.
- At 08:59 it ends one minute later: the preset means "until the working day starts".
- At 09:00 sharp, and at any later time of the day, it ends at 09:00 the next day.
- There is no working-week calendar, so on Friday evening "Until tomorrow 09:00" ends on Saturday at 09:00. For a
  weekend, use `week_start`, which ends on Monday at 09:00.
- The start is the time on the clock on the day of the end. A start that the clocks skip moves forward by the change:
  02:30 on the night the clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00 is 03:30. A start that the clocks show twice, when they go
  back, is the first of the two.

The end is stored as a time. A later change of the settings or of a time zone never moves a Snooze already set, and the
Snooze ends like any other: if Alerts still fire, the Alert Group is Firing again without an Owner, with a Loud message.

**Time zone.** The preset counts in the time zone that the request names in `time_zone`. Without one, it counts in the
profile time zone of the user who snoozes, also through a Personal access token, and otherwise in the Organization's
time zone (`organization.time_zone`). A Service account has no profile, so it always gets the Organization's. A press on
a button in a messenger and a Text command carry no time zone, so they count in the profile time zone of the linked user
who pressed or wrote, and otherwise in the Organization's.

**Settings.** Two Organization settings define the presets, as the fields `workday_start` and `week_start` of the
organization in the API:

`organization.workday_start`
:   default: `09:00`

    The start of the working day, `HH:MM` on the 24-hour clock.

`organization.week_start`
:   default: `monday`

    The first day of the week, `monday` to `sunday`.

**API.** A Snooze takes `preset`, `tomorrow` or `week_start`, as a third choice beside `until` and `no_end`, with an
optional `time_zone`:

```json
{"preset": "tomorrow", "time_zone": "Europe/Berlin"}
```

A `time_zone` without `preset` is refused with `422` `unsupported`, and a time zone Muster does not know with `422`
`invalid_format`. A bulk Snooze with a preset computes the end once, so every Alert Group gets the same end.
`GET /api/v1/snooze-presets`, with an optional `time_zone`, answers the end that each preset would set now and the time
zone it used; it needs the Permission to snooze and changes nothing. The Audit log entry of a preset Snooze names the
preset and the time zone beside the end. See the [API reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/api.md).

#### In the web UI

The Snooze dialog of an Alert Group offers both presets after the Route's Snooze durations and before "Until" and "No
end", also on a Route without durations; the bulk Snooze of the list, which has no durations, offers them first. Under
each preset the dialog shows the end it would set now, such as "Ends Oct 20, 2026, 09:00": Muster computes it when the
dialog opens, on its own clock and in your time zone (the one of your profile, else your browser's), and the dialog sends
that time zone with the preset. Admins set the start of the working day and the first day of the week on Organization →
General. In the profile, a hint under the time zone says that presets pressed in messengers end in that time zone, and
in the Organization's while the profile follows the browser.

#### In messengers

On a Route with Snooze durations, the Root message of a firing or an acknowledged Alert Group offers both presets as
two more Snooze buttons after the durations: "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00", or «До завтра 09:00» and
«До понедельника 09:00» on a Route in Russian. The time is `organization.workday_start` and the day
`organization.week_start`, so with the week starting on Sunday the second button reads "Until Sunday 09:00". A snoozed
Alert Group offers no Snooze button, and a Route without Snooze durations offers no preset either, because an empty
`route.snooze_durations` means no Snooze from messengers. Telegram shows the presets on a row of their own under the
durations, and a bridge with a limit on buttons drops them first; see
[Bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/bridge.md#what-muster-posts). Slack offers the durations and then the presets as the options of
one **Snooze…** menu, since its web client folds the buttons beyond five in a row.

The labels are part of the message. After a change of `organization.workday_start` or `organization.week_start`, each
Root message shows the new labels at its next update, and a press on a button shown before the change already ends at
the new start of the working day: the preset is computed when the command runs. On a bridge without buttons, the presets
are [Text commands](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#text-commands).

### Who may

A **Responder** or an **Admin** may acknowledge, resolve, snooze and add Notes. A **Viewer** may read and may not act:
the command is refused. A **Service account** may run the commands its Role allows, except Acknowledge and Still on it,
because an Owner is always a User. A Personal access token acts as its User, with at most that User's Permissions. Every
command is recorded in the Audit log with its actor and the Transport.

## Where a command comes from

The **Transport** is the way a command reaches Muster. It is recorded with the command, and Muster applies the same rules
to all of them.

Web UI
:   how: buttons on the Alert Group page and in the list, with dialogs for Snooze and Resolve · notes: everything above,
    including bulk commands, Notes and Unresolve

API
:   how: `POST` to `/api/v1/alert-groups/{id}/acknowledge` and its siblings, with a session or a token · notes: the
    same; see the [API reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/api.md)

Mattermost
:   how: a button on the message · notes: Acknowledge, Unacknowledge, Resolve, Snooze, Unsnooze, Still on it

Slack
:   how: a button on the message, and the **Snooze…** menu with the durations and then the presets · notes: the same

Telegram
:   how: an inline button on the message · notes: the same

Bridge
:   how: a button on the message, if the bridge declares `buttons`; or a **Text command** in the Thread, if it declares
    `thread_messages` · notes: the same

`system`
:   how: Muster itself · notes: the automatic transitions above, shown in the Timeline

Messengers never offer Unresolve or Notes, and never a Snooze with no end. A person who presses a button in a messenger
must have linked their messenger account to their Muster user; see [Link your messenger
accounts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/account-links.md). A press from an unlinked account changes nothing, and the person is told
privately how to link it.

### What each button does

The buttons of a Root message depend on the status of its Alert Group:

| Status | Buttons |
|---|---|
| Firing | **Ack**, **Resolve**, **Snooze** |
| Acknowledged | **Unack**, **Resolve**, **Snooze** |
| Snoozed | **Ack**, **Unsnooze**, **Resolve** |
| Resolved | none; a link "Open in Muster" |

- **Ack** takes the Alert Group: you become its Owner, the Reminders start, and the message shows who has it. If somebody
  else has it, Ack takes it over from them.
- **Unack** gives it back. The Alert Group becomes Firing again with no Owner, and the ack timeout starts over.
- **Resolve** closes the Alert Group by hand. If Alerts still fire, the message shows "⚠ N alerts still firing in
  Alertmanager", and after the Grace period the Alerts that still fire start a new Alert Group.
- **Snooze** sets it aside. It offers the Route's Snooze durations, such as 1 hour, 4 hours and 24 hours, one choice for
  each, then the two [Snooze presets](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#in-messengers) "Until tomorrow 09:00" and "Until Monday 09:00", which end at the
  next start of the working day, or at its start on the first day of the week, in your profile time zone, or else the
  Organization's. When the time is up and Alerts still fire, the Alert Group comes back Firing and a Loud message says
  so.
- **Unsnooze** ends the Snooze early. The Alert Group becomes Firing again.
- On a **Reminder**, **Still on it** tells Muster you are still handling the Alert Group, and **Unack** gives it up.
- A **Storm summary** and an ack timeout notice carry only links to Muster. A test message carries the buttons of its
  status, but pressing them changes nothing: you get "This is a test message; nothing was changed".

A press edits the Root message to show the result. A press that Muster refuses, such as a Resolve by a Viewer, is answered
privately to the person who pressed, and nothing changes.

### Text commands

Some messengers have no buttons, or a bridge does not offer them. A **Text command** is a Command written as a reply in a
Thread. Only a **Bridge** Destination takes them, and only when the bridge declares `thread_messages`. A Root message
that is not resolved then ends with a line such as "Reply in the Thread: ack · resolve · snooze 1h".

A reply is a Text command when its whole text, trimmed, in any case and with an optional leading `/`, is one of:

| Text command | Same in Russian | Command |
|---|---|---|
| `ack` | `взял` | Acknowledge |
| `unack` | `отпускаю` | Unacknowledge |
| `resolve` | `решено` | Resolve |
| `snooze <duration>` | `отложить <duration>` | Snooze |
| `unsnooze` | `вернуть` | Unsnooze |
| `still on it` | `ещё работаю` (also `еще работаю`) | Still on it |

The `<duration>` is one of the Route's Snooze durations, written in minutes, hours or days: `30m`, `4h` or `1d`, and
`30м`, `4ч` or `1д` in Russian. It can also name a [Snooze preset](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/statuses-and-commands.md#snooze-presets): `tomorrow` (`завтра`) for the next
start of the working day, or the first day of the week (`organization.week_start`), such as `monday` (`понедельник`),
for the start of the working day on that day. So `snooze tomorrow`, `/Snooze Tomorrow` and `отложить понедельник` (with
the week starting on Monday) all work. A day is written as it stands alone: `понедельник`, `вторник`, `среда`,
`четверг`, `пятница`, `суббота`, `воскресенье`. Every word works whatever the Route's language is. The writer needs an
Account link, and the same permissions as for a button.

Muster answers a Text command in the Thread, for example "Done: Acknowledged #42", or with the reason it refused. A
duration that is not one of the Route's, or a day other than the first day of the week, is answered with what the Route
offers: "Snooze for one of: 1h, 4h, 24h, tomorrow, monday". The sentence and the durations are in the writer's profile
language, and the two preset words in the Route's language. A Route without Snooze durations takes no preset either, and
answers "This Alert Group's Route has no Snooze durations; nothing was changed." **Any other text is ignored and never
answered**, so people can talk in the Thread. The Thread of an older Root message works too: a Text command there acts
on the Alert Group like any other, also when the message is past its
[edit window](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/bridge.md#edit-windows). A Text command older than an hour (`bridge.event_max_age`) is
dropped. If the bridge forwards only the messages that mention its bot, the line says "mentioning the bot", and the
command must mention it. See [Write a bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/write-a-bridge.md#events) for how a bridge reports a Thread
message.

## Ack timeouts, Reminders and auto-unacknowledge

Three timers make sure nobody forgets: one for an Alert Group nobody has taken, one for an Alert Group somebody took and
then went quiet, and an optional one that takes the Alert Group back. They are Route settings; the On-call profile turns
the first two on and the Informational profile turns everything off.

### Ack timeout

The ack timeout runs while an Alert Group is Firing. It starts at the Alert Group's first Publication in a Destination, and
starts over each time it becomes Firing again. Acknowledge, Snooze and Resolve stop it.

When nobody acknowledges, Muster sends up to three **notices**, at doubling intervals from the Route's first interval
(`route.ack_timeout`, 15 minutes on an On-call Route). With 15 minutes they come at 15, 45 and 105 minutes after the start.
Each is a Loud Thread reply that Mentions whom the Destination's `ack_timeout` setting says. After the last notice the
Alert Group is **Unclaimed**: its message shows "⚠ Nobody has taken this", and the Alert Group list has an Unclaimed
filter, column and badge. Unclaimed ends when the Alert Group stops being Firing.

An Alert Group that has not been published, as when its Route has no Destination or only Broken ones, has no ack timeout
until its first Publication.

### Reminders

When somebody acknowledges, Muster reminds the Owner while the Alert Group stays open (`route.reminders`, on an On-call
Route). The first **Reminder** comes 4 hours after the acknowledgement, and each next interval doubles up to 24 hours: at 4,
12, 28 and 52 hours, then every 24 hours. Each is a Loud Thread reply that Mentions the Owner, with the buttons **Still
on it** and **Unack**.

- **Still on it** is recorded in the Timeline and does not change the interval. The Owner can also answer from the Alert
  Group page or the API.
- A **Takeover** starts the Reminders over for the new Owner. A Reopen into acknowledged continues them. A snoozed Alert
  Group gets none. There are no quiet hours.
- An Owner who is disabled or deleted loses the acknowledgement: the Alert Group becomes Firing without an Owner, and the
  ack timeout starts over.
- After Muster was down, the overdue notices of one Alert Group collapse into one Loud Thread reply that says how many
  were missed.
- Buttons on Reminders are signed like the others, but are not updated after a key rotation. Once the old key is removed,
  a press is answered "This button has expired; use the buttons on the Alert Group's message".

### Auto-unacknowledge

If an Owner goes home and says nothing, the Alert Group would stay acknowledged forever. **Auto-unacknowledge**
(`route.auto_unacknowledge`, off by default) takes it back. The Owner answers a Reminder by pressing **Still on it**, by
running any command on the Alert Group or by adding a Note before the next Reminder is due. When the Owner has answered
neither of the last two Reminders (`timers.auto_unacknowledge_after`), the next Reminder is not sent. Instead Muster
unacknowledges the Alert Group with the reason "No answer to the last two Reminders". It becomes Firing without an Owner,
a Loud Thread reply gives the reason and Mentions the Owner, and the ack timeout starts over.

For example, Carol acknowledges at 10:00 and goes home. She answers neither the Reminder at 14:00 nor the one at 22:00.
At 14:00 the next day, instead of a third Reminder, Muster unacknowledges the Alert Group and Mentions Carol, and the
ack timeout notices begin again.

The Alert Group page shows the next scheduled notice or Reminder.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/broken-destinations.md -->
# Broken Destinations

A Destination is **Broken** when Muster has decided that it cannot deliver there until something changes: the messenger
refused the bot for good, or the messenger kept failing until Muster ran out of patience. A Broken Destination is not an
error to dismiss. It means that the people it serves are not seeing their alerts, so Muster raises an alert about it.

This page explains when a Destination becomes Broken, what Muster does meanwhile, and how it recovers. For the steps
when `MusterDestinationBroken` fires, use the [runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterDestinationBroken.md).

## When a Destination becomes Broken

Every failed attempt is sorted into a class, and the class decides what happens:

Retry after
:   examples: the messenger answers `429` and says how long to wait

    Muster waits exactly that long and then sends the latest state. It is not counted as an attempt.

Transient
:   examples: a `5xx`, a timeout, a network error

    Muster retries with exponential backoff and jitter, from 2 seconds up to 5 minutes. After **10 attempts within 30
    minutes** (`delivery.transient_budget`) the Destination becomes Broken as *unavailable*.

Fatal
:   examples: the messenger refuses the bot or the request for good

    The Destination becomes Broken **at once**.

Unknown
:   examples: an answer Muster does not recognize

    Not retried. That one delivery ends as *Not delivered*, and the Destination stays healthy.

What is Fatal depends on the messenger:

- **Mattermost**: `401` or `403`, such as an invalid token or a bot removed from the channel, and `404` for the channel,
  which is not found or archived.
- **Slack**: a token that Slack refuses (`invalid_auth`, `token_revoked`, `token_expired` and the like), a missing
  scope, and a channel the bot cannot use: `channel_not_found`, `not_in_channel` for a bot removed from the channel, and
  `is_archived`. A `429` is not Fatal: Muster holds the whole Connection for the seconds Slack asks.
- **Telegram**: `401`, and "bot was kicked" or missing rights, such as a bot that lost its admin rights in the channel.
- **Bridge**: the bridge answers `forbidden`, for example because the bot was removed from the channel; the bridge's own
  text becomes the reason. A bridge that does not answer at all becomes Broken through the Transient budget.
- **Outgoing webhook**: `401`, `403`, `404` and `410`, and a request that the Organization's outbound address policy blocks,
  since every later request would be blocked too.

Several things look like trouble and do **not** make a Destination Broken:

- A deleted Root message. Muster posts the Alert Group again once, Quietly, with the note "The previous message was
  deleted at HH:MM"; if that one is deleted too, the pair is marked "deleted in the messenger" and left alone. In Slack
  this holds while the bot is still in the channel and the channel is not archived; see [Edits and deleted Root
  messages](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/slack.md#edits-and-deleted-root-messages).
- A Telegram Thread that lost the automatic copy of its Root message. The delivery state shows "Thread not attached".
- A delivery that ends as Not delivered, such as a template that failed or a request the receiver rejected with `400`.
- A Bridge Connection whose bridge cannot be reached. The Connection does not become Broken itself; its Destinations do,
  through their own deliveries, and its Connection check shows the cause.
- Failed polls of a bridge or of Telegram. The poller backs off.

## What you see

- **The Destination and its Routes** show a banner: "Broken since HH:MM: {reason}. Muster tries again every 5 minutes."
  The reason is the error the messenger answered, or "unavailable after repeated failures" and the last error.
- **The Internal alert** `MusterDestinationBroken` is raised, with the severity critical and the labels `destination` and
  `destination_name`. Muster routes it by your Routes like any other Alert, so a Route for Internal alerts should lead to
  a Destination of **another kind** than the one that failed: if all your Telegram Destinations are Broken because
  Telegram is unreachable, an alert that goes to Telegram says nothing. See [Routes and Group
  keys](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/concepts/routes-and-group-keys.md#examples).
- **The chart rule** `MusterDestinationBroken` is the backup for when Muster cannot deliver its own alert. Send it through
  an Alertmanager route that bypasses Muster. See [Internal alerts](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/internal-alerts.md) and the
  [metrics](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/metrics.md).
- The **Alert Groups** whose delivery waits show a delivery problem. The Alert Group list has the filter **Delivery
  problem**, and the page of each shows the state "Waiting: {Destination} is Broken".
- The **System status** page lists the Broken Destinations and since when.

## What Muster does meanwhile

Everything except the delivery to that Destination goes on: ingestion, routing, Alert Groups, commands from the web UI
and the API, timers, and every other Destination.

- **Deliveries wait instead of failing.** Nothing is dropped, and Muster does not spend retries on a Destination it knows
  is down.
- **Muster probes the Destination every 5 minutes** (`delivery.broken_probe_interval`). If a delivery is waiting, the
  probe is an attempt at the oldest one. If nothing is waiting, the probe is the **Destination check**, which asks the
  messenger whether the bot can still reach and post to the channel, without posting. An outgoing webhook has no
  Destination check, so its next delivery is the probe.
- **A new Alert Group is created and shown in Muster** as usual, but its first Publication waits. Its ack timeout does not
  start until it is published, so a Route whose only Destinations are Broken sends no notices.

## Recovery

The Broken state ends when **any** of these succeeds:

- the automatic probe;
- **Check** on the Destination page, which runs the Destination check at once;
- **Send test message** on the Destination page, when every step succeeds.

Fix the cause first. Typical fixes are a replaced bot token, adding the bot back to the channel or giving it its admin
rights again, enabling comments on a Telegram channel, correcting the address or the proxy of the Connection or the
**Outbound addresses** policy, or waiting out a messenger outage. When the fix is made, press **Check**; if you do
nothing, the next probe notices by itself, with no Alert Group activity needed. The Internal alert then resolves.

### What is sent after recovery

Muster sends only the **current state**. It does not replay what it missed.

| What happened during the outage | After recovery |
|---|---|
| An Alert Group started and is still firing | It is published as a Loud new message. |
| An Alert Group started and is no longer firing, but still open | It is published Quietly. |
| An Alert Group was already published, then changed | Its Root message is edited once to the current state, with no Thread reply. |
| An Alert Group started and resolved during the outage | It is **not** published; it stays in the Timeline and in the web UI. |
| Thread replies came due | They are not sent. |

Urgent Alert Groups are published first, within the Destination's rate limits.

An **outgoing webhook in events mode** is the exception: it is a stream of events, so every event that came due during the
outage is sent after recovery, in order per Alert Group, with none dropped and no age limit. An outgoing webhook in
template mode sends only the current state, like a messenger.

If an Alert Group resolved while its first Publication was still waiting for a retry, but the Destination was not yet
Broken, it is still posted, Quietly, with the note "Delivered late: started HH:MM, resolved HH:MM while this Destination
was unavailable".

## Republishing past an edit window

Muster edits a Root message for as long as its Alert Group is open, which can take days. Whether a messenger lets it
depends on the messenger. This is not about a Broken Destination, but the messages that Muster can no longer edit look
similar from the outside, so here is the whole picture.

Telegram
:   None for the bot's own messages. A bot may edit them at any age, so Muster never republishes because of age.

Slack
:   None known for a bot's own messages. Whether a window that a workspace sets applies to a bot's messages hours or
    days old has not been verified; an edit Slack refuses ends that delivery as Not delivered.

Mattermost
:   The server setting `ServiceSettings.PostEditTimeLimit`, which is unlimited (`-1`) by default. Keep the default. If
    an administrator sets a limit, Muster's edits of older Root messages may be refused, and what Mattermost then
    answers has not been verified. See [Keep posts editable](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/mattermost.md#keep-posts-editable).

Bridge
:   The bridge declares it in its info, as `limits.edit_max_age_seconds`, or declares none.

Outgoing webhook
:   Muster does not know the chat's rules. In template mode an `update` request that the chat refuses ends as Not
    delivered or Broken by the usual classes.

For a **Bridge** with an edit window, Muster stops editing a Root message 60 seconds before the window closes
(`bridge.edit_window_margin`). After that:

- A change that keeps the status of the Alert Group, such as new Alerts or Alerts that resolve, reaches only the Thread.
  The old Root message keeps the state of its last edit.
- A **change of status**, such as Acknowledge, Resolve, Snooze or a Reopen, makes Muster publish a **new Root message**
  Quietly, in the same channel, and reply under the old one: "This message is no longer updated. The current one:
  {link}". Later Thread replies go under the new Root message.
- The old message keeps working: a press on its buttons, or a Text command in its Thread, still acts on the Alert Group.
- The Alert Group page shows "Past the edit window: updated on the next change of status" until then.

A bridge may also refuse an edit before the declared time, with the reason `edit_window_closed`. Muster treats that as the
end of the window, not as a deletion. See [Edit windows](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/bridge.md#edit-windows) for the details.

## After you delete a Destination

A deleted Destination receives one last edit of each open Root message, "No longer updated here; current state in Muster:
{link}", and nothing after that. For a Bridge Root message past its edit window, the last edit is a Thread reply with
the same text. An outgoing webhook in events mode sends no final event, and its queued events end as Not delivered.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/backup-and-restore.md -->
# Backup and restore

Muster keeps all its state in PostgreSQL, and encrypts its secrets with the [master keys](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md) from the
environment. Neither the Helm chart nor the compose example backs up anything, so you back up two things, **separately**:

The database
:   Holds Integrations, Routes, Alert Groups, people, the Audit log and every Secret, encrypted.

    Without it, everything is gone.

The master keys (`MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS`)
:   Hold the keys that decrypt the Secrets and sign the buttons in messages.

    Without them, Muster refuses to start on the database, and its encrypted Secrets cannot be read.

## Why they are kept apart

A database backup alone reveals no bot token, OIDC client secret or proxy password, because Muster encrypts them before
they reach the database. A backup together with the master keys reveals all of them. Store the two in different places
and give them different access: the dump in your backup storage, the keys where you keep your other secrets, such as a
password manager or the secret store of your cluster.

Without the master key that wrote the database, Muster refuses to start on it, and nobody can read the Secrets in it.
Muster cannot recover them, and it has no way to start that database again with a new key: keep the key safe.

After a [key rotation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md), back up the new key list too. A backup taken before the rotation needs the old
key to restore.

## Back up the database

Muster has no backup format of its own. Use the tools of PostgreSQL:

- **A dump.** `pg_dump` writes a consistent copy while Muster runs:

    ```sh
    pg_dump --format=custom --file=muster-$(date +%F).dump "$MUSTER_DATABASE_URL"
    ```

    With the compose example, run it in the database container:

    ```sh
    docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U muster --format=custom muster > muster-$(date +%F).dump
    ```

- **Continuous backup.** With CloudNativePG, add `spec.backup` to the `Cluster`; see [the
  database](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/database.md#cloudnativepg). A managed PostgreSQL offers its own snapshots and point-in-time
  recovery. Either is better than a nightly dump when you cannot lose an hour of Alert Groups.

Take a backup before every [upgrade](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md), and test a restore before you rely on it.

## Restore

1. Stop every Muster replica. In Kubernetes, scale the Deployment to 0; with compose, stop the `muster` service.
2. Restore the database into an empty database. For a dump:

    ```sh
    pg_restore --clean --if-exists --no-owner --dbname="$MUSTER_DATABASE_URL" muster-2026-10-19.dump
    ```

    A CloudNativePG or managed restore creates a new cluster from the backup; point `database.host` at it. When the
    chart reads the database from the Secret that CloudNativePG generates, point `database.existingSecret` at the new
    cluster's `-app` Secret too: it holds a new password and, in its `uri`, the new host.
3. Put the **same master keys** back into `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS`. The key that was active when the backup was taken must be
   in the list. Keys are identified by their material, so any copy of the same key works.
4. Start Muster, in the version that wrote the backup or in a newer one that the [upgrade rules](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md#the-rules)
   allow. It applies the migrations that are
   missing (see [Upgrades](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md#migrations)) and checks the key canary. A wrong or missing key stops the start with
   "master key does not match the database".
5. Run `muster doctor` with the same environment as the server, and read every line. See [the
   CLI](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md#muster-doctor).

After the restore, Muster treats the time since the last "alive" mark as downtime. For a while, the web UI says that
Muster is recovering and its data may be incomplete, and overdue timers fire once, collapsed. That is expected.

## What to check

- `muster doctor` exits 0. The `key_canary` line is `OK`, which proves that the keys match the database. The `keyring`
  line is `OK` when no older key is in use; it is `WARN` while a Secret or an open Root message still needs an older key,
  and it says when a key is no longer used and can be [removed](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md#remove-the-old-key).
- **Organization → System status** shows one Leader and every replica, and no Destination you did not expect as Broken.
- Open an Alert Group and press a button in its messenger message. A press works only when the master keys are right.
- Messengers and Alertmanagers reach the restored Muster at `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` and `MUSTER_INGEST_URL`. If you
  restored into an installation with other addresses, change them in the environment and check the Connections.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md -->
# Upgrades

Muster follows semantic versioning (`major.minor.patch`). A release publishes the container image
`ghcr.io/muster-io/muster`, binaries, and the Helm chart as an OCI artifact in the same registry. The changelog of each
release is on the releases page of the repository, written from the commit messages.

## The rules

- **Patch and minor versions.** Update to the next version, or to any patch version of the same minor version.
- **Rolling updates only between adjacent minor versions.** From 1.4.x to 1.5.x, replica by replica, is supported. From
  1.4.x to 1.7.x is not: go through 1.5 and 1.6, or stop every replica before you start the new version.
- **Back up first.** Take a [database backup](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/backup-and-restore.md) before every upgrade, because of the next rule.
- **No downgrades.** Migrations only go forward in production. A binary refuses to start on a schema newer than it knows
  and names both versions. To go back, restore the backup you took before the upgrade, together with the master keys of
  that time, and run the old version on it. Everything written since is lost.
- Read the release notes of every version you skip. Settings that change are named there.

## Upgrade with Helm

1. Take a backup.
2. Change the version: `helm upgrade muster oci://ghcr.io/muster-io/charts/muster --version <version> -n muster -f values.yaml`.
   The chart's `image.tag` defaults to its `appVersion`, so the chart and the image move together. If you pin
   `image.tag`, change it too.
3. Watch the rollout: `kubectl -n muster rollout status deploy/muster`.
4. Run `muster doctor` (see [the CLI](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md#muster-doctor)) and open **Organization → System status**: it shows the
   version and commit that serve the page, and under *Replicas* which replica is the Leader.

The chart does not migrate in the server. Each new pod runs `muster migrate` in an **init container** before its server
container starts, and `MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START` stays off. The pods of a rollout do not migrate at once, because
migrations run under a database lock. Kubernetes starts a new pod before it stops an old one, so the web UI and
ingestion stay up with one replica too; run two replicas with a
[PodDisruptionBudget](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/high-availability.md#two-replicas) if you also want to survive the loss of a node.

## Upgrade with Docker Compose

The compose example sets `MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START` to `true`: the server migrates when it starts. Take a backup, change
the image (set `MUSTER_IMAGE`, or download the compose file of the new release), and run `docker compose up -d`. With a
single replica nothing else is needed.

## Migrations

Migrations are SQL files built into the binary. They run through `muster migrate` or, when
`MUSTER_MIGRATE_ON_START` is `true`, at server start, in both cases under a session advisory lock and with the
applied versions in the log.

Every migration follows **expand and contract**: a release only adds what the previous release can ignore, and removes
what the previous release no longer uses in a later release. That is why a rolling update between adjacent minor
versions works: while the new schema is in place, the replicas of the old version still run on it.

To migrate before you update the servers, run the command of the new version with the environment of the server:

```sh
muster migrate
```

It needs the database settings and `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS` of the server (see [the CLI](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md#environment)). It exits non-zero
on a schema newer than the binary knows.

## During a rolling update

Replicas of two adjacent minor versions serve at the same time, and either may be the Leader. Do not leave an
installation in this state: finish the rollout.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md -->
# Key rotation

Muster encrypts its Secrets and signs the buttons of its messages with the **master keys** in `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS`. These
keys form the Keyring; one of them is **active** and encrypts and signs, and all of them can still decrypt and verify.
Which key is active is stored in the database, not in the environment. Muster never generates a master key and never
writes the environment: you add a new key yourself, then tell Muster to use it.

Rotate when a key may have leaked, when a person who knew it leaves, or on a schedule you keep. The rotation takes two
deliberate steps, so that a rolling restart never leaves a replica unable to read what another one wrote.

## Step 1: add the new key everywhere

1. Generate a key: `openssl rand -base64 32`.
2. Add it to `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS`, **after** the current key, separated by a comma. With the Helm chart the value comes
   from the key `secret-keys` of your Secret (`masterKeysKey`); `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS_FILE` takes one key per line.
3. Roll the change out to every replica. Muster applies a changed environment only on start, so restart the pods.

Both keys stay in the list. The key that is active does not change yet, and nothing is re-encrypted.

Each replica records the key ids it holds every 30 seconds, and counts as live while its record is younger than 2
minutes. Open **Organization → Keyring**. It lists every key by its id, which one is *Active*, and for each key *Held by*
the replicas that have it and *Missing on* those that do not. The new key has the state **Not active yet**, because it
has never been active. Muster never calls such a key removable.

## Step 2: activate it

Run the command with the same environment as the server (see [the CLI](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md#muster-secrets-rotate-key)), giving the
id of the new key as the Keyring page shows it:

```sh
muster secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor alice
```

`--actor` names who runs the command and goes to the Audit log. Muster refuses to activate a key while a live replica
does not hold it, names those replicas, and exits 1. Wait until the Keyring page shows no replica as *Missing on*, or
until the replica that lacks the key stops being live, and run the command again.

When every live replica holds the key, one transaction:

- makes the key active,
- re-encrypts every stored Secret and the key canary with it, and
- records `keyring.key_activated` in the Audit log.

The replicas switch to the key without a restart. Then the Leader recomputes the message of every open Alert Group whose
buttons the old key signed, so that the delivery worker edits each Root message and signs its buttons with the new key.
The edits go through the usual limits of the messengers, so a large backlog takes a while.

## Remove the old key

The old key is still needed while a Secret or an open Root message depends on it. The Keyring page shows each older
key as *Still needed* until nothing does; then it says **Key `<id>` is no longer used and can be removed from
MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS.** `muster doctor` prints the same on its `keyring` line, with the number of encrypted values and
open Root messages that still need each key. Only a key that was active before is ever called removable.

Then remove the key from `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS` and roll the change out. Removing the key before Muster says so breaks
what still depends on it; the start of a replica that lacks the *active* key fails with "master key does not match the
database".

Keep the old key in your records until the backups that need it are gone: a [backup](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/backup-and-restore.md) taken before
the rotation restores only with the key that was active then.

## What stops working when the old key goes

- **Buttons in Thread replies.** Muster re-signs only the buttons of Root messages. A Reminder, for example, is a Thread
  reply, and keeps the signature it was sent with. Once the old key is gone, a press on such a button is answered
  privately: "This button has expired; use the buttons on the Alert Group's message". Nothing changes in the Alert
  Group, and the Root message works.
- **Web pages that were open before the rotation.** The CSRF token that a web page sends with each change carries the id of
  the key that signed it, and verifies while Muster holds that key. A page that has been open since before the rotation
  has the old token. Once the old key is gone, the next change from that page is refused (`403`, `csrf_invalid`) and the
  page says "The page is out of date. Reload it and try again." Reload the page, and it works again with a token of the
  new key. Nobody has to sign in again.

Nothing else changes: Personal access tokens and Service account tokens are stored as hashes and are not affected, and the
Signing secret of an outgoing webhook Destination does not change (Muster only re-encrypts it).

## If something goes wrong

`Replicas {names} do not hold key {id} yet.`
:   cause: a live replica has not restarted with the new key · what to do: finish the rollout, or wait until the record
    of a gone replica expires

`key {id} is not in the master keys of this process`
:   cause: you ran the command without the new key in `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS` · what to do: give the command the same
    environment as the server

A replica stops with "master key does not match the database"
:   cause: it lacks the active key · what to do: add the key back to its environment

Exit code 2
:   cause: `--activate` or `--actor` is missing · what to do: add the flag

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/high-availability.md -->
# High availability

Run more than one replica of Muster when you want the web UI, ingestion and delivery to survive the loss of a node or
a restart. The Helm chart defaults to one replica, and the compose example runs one. Two replicas with a
PodDisruptionBudget are an option, not a requirement.

## All replicas are active

Every replica serves the web UI, the API and ingestion, and runs the workers for ingestion, delivery and timers. The
workers claim rows from PostgreSQL with a lease, so a timer such as an ack timeout, a Reminder or the end of a Snooze
fires on whichever replica is free. A replica that stalls delays nothing beyond its lease.

## The Leader

A few tasks must run **once**, not once per replica. One replica, the **Leader**, runs only those. The list is closed:

| Task | What it does |
|---|---|
| Telegram polling | long polling of `getUpdates` for Connections in that update mode; Telegram answers `409` to a second poller |
| Bridge polling | polls the events of Bridge Connections in the `poll` event delivery mode, with one cursor per Connection |
| Slack's Socket Mode | holds one Socket Mode connection per Slack Connection in the `socket` event mode; presses made during a handover are lost, the `http` event mode avoids that |
| Heartbeat and Stale checks | find Integrations that are Heartbeat lost and Alerts that went Stale |
| partitions and retention | create partitions ahead of time, drop expired ones, and delete what the retention periods remove |
| pruning | removes ended sessions, expired requests and links, the records of gone replicas, and the Request log past its bounds |
| database gauges | the metrics computed from the database: open Alert Groups, the ingestion backlog, delivery queues, Broken Destinations, Storms |
| the "alive" mark | every 30 seconds, so that a restarted Muster knows how long it was down |
| the outgoing heartbeat | the call to your [dead man's switch](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/outgoing-heartbeat.md) |
| OIDC secret expiry check | raises `MusterOIDCSecretExpiring` |
| re-render after a key rotation | re-signs the buttons of open Root messages ([Key rotation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md)) |

Nothing else depends on the Leader. Every task is safe to run twice, because a handover can overlap for a moment.

### How a replica becomes Leader

The Leader holds a **session advisory lock** in PostgreSQL on a dedicated connection, the *session connection*. Every
replica tries to take the lock every `leader.ping_interval` (5 seconds); one succeeds. The Leader proves that it still
holds the lock by pinging over that session at the same interval. If no ping succeeds for `leader.fencing_timeout` (15
seconds), it stops all Leader tasks and closes the connection, and it may compete for the lock again later.

When a Leader crashes, its connection closes and PostgreSQL releases the lock at once. When its node disappears or the
network splits, PostgreSQL would keep the session for hours by default. Muster sets `idle_session_timeout` on the lock
session and TCP keepalives, so PostgreSQL ends a silent session and releases the lock within `leader.server_bound` (30
seconds). The fencing timeout is shorter than that, so the old Leader normally stops before another replica can take
over. The values are built in; they are not settings.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as "Replica A (Leader)"
  participant PG as "PostgreSQL"
  participant B as "Replica B"
  A->>PG: "ping over the lock session, every 5 s"
  B->>PG: "try the lock, every 5 s: taken"
  Note over A: "the node of A is lost"
  Note over A: "A stops its Leader tasks after 15 s without a ping"
  PG-->>PG: "ends the silent session within 30 s, the lock is free"
  B->>PG: "try the lock: acquired"
  Note over B: "B is the Leader: muster_leader is 1"
  B->>PG: "writes the alive mark, runs the Leader tasks"
```

A handover after the loss of a node takes well under a minute. During it, Telegram and Bridge polling, Slack's Socket
Mode connections, the periodic checks and the outgoing heartbeat pause. Ingestion, delivery and timers do not. Telegram
and the bridges keep what arrives meanwhile. A press made in Socket Mode before the new Leader connects is lost and
its person sees Slack's error: Muster does not count on Slack to send it again.

### When no replica leads

The gauge `muster_leader` is 1 on the Leader and 0 on the others. When the "alive" mark is older than 2 minutes
(`leader.absence_notice`), the web UI shows a notice that no replica is leading. The chart rule `MusterNoLeader` fires
when no replica has led for 2 minutes; see [its runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterNoLeader.md).

While there is no Leader:

- **Bridge** Connections in the `poll` mode and Telegram Connections in the long polling mode receive no button presses and
  no Text commands. When a Leader returns, a Bridge press or Text command older than `bridge.event_max_age` (1 hour) is
  dropped unanswered; a Telegram press is dropped unanswered when the Connection received no updates for longer than
  `telegram.press_max_age` (1 hour) before it. Connections in the `push` mode of a Bridge and the webhook mode of
  Telegram keep working.
- Slack Connections in the `socket` event mode hold no Socket Mode connection: a press made meanwhile is lost, and the
  person sees Slack's error. Connections in the `http` event mode keep working.
- No Integration becomes Heartbeat lost and no Alert goes Stale.
- Partition maintenance, retention and pruning pause; the gauges that only the Leader exports go stale.
- The outgoing heartbeat stops, so a [dead man's switch](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/outgoing-heartbeat.md) alerts you.

Ingestion, delivery, timers, the web UI and the API keep working.

### After downtime

When every replica was down, the next Leader reads the "alive" mark, records the period, and adds a Timeline entry to open
Alert Groups. Timers that came due during the downtime fire once, collapsed. For a while the web UI says Muster is
recovering.

## The session connection

The Leader lock and the `LISTEN` connections need a real session. If the main database connection goes through PgBouncer
in transaction mode, set `MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_HOST` and `MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_PORT` (in the chart,
`database.sessionHost` and `database.sessionPort`), or `MUSTER_DATABASE_SESSION_URL`, to an endpoint that reaches
PostgreSQL directly or through a pooler in session mode. At start, Muster checks that advisory locks and `LISTEN` work
over it and stops with an error that names the setting otherwise. See [PgBouncer](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/database.md#pgbouncer).

## Two replicas

In the Helm values:

```yaml
replicas: 2
podDisruptionBudget:
  enabled: true
  maxUnavailable: 1
```

The PodDisruptionBudget keeps a node drain from stopping both pods at once. Spread the pods over nodes with
`topologySpreadConstraints` or `affinity`. See [Install with Helm](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/helm.md) for the other values. PostgreSQL
is the single stateful component, so its own availability, such as a CloudNativePG cluster with two instances, sets the
limit of the installation.

Replicas of different minor versions run side by side only during a rolling [upgrade](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md#the-rules).

## Clocks

Replicas share one database and take the time from their own system clocks. Run NTP, or the time service of your cloud
provider, on **every node** and on the database server. A replica measures its clock against the database every minute and
exports it as `muster_clock_skew_seconds`; it logs a warning above `process.clock_skew_warning` (2 seconds), and the chart
rule `MusterClockSkew` fires after 5 minutes.

A skew moves the timestamps a replica writes and the timers and windows it evaluates, and it can make TOTP codes, OIDC ID
tokens and the timestamps of outgoing webhook signatures fail. It can also make the lease of a row or of the Leader lock
expire too early or too late, so that work runs twice or waits. See the [MusterClockSkew
runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/MusterClockSkew.md), and check the clock with [`muster doctor`](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md#muster-doctor).

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/monitoring.md -->
# Monitoring

Muster exports Prometheus metrics, ships alert rules and a Grafana dashboard in its Helm chart, and raises Internal
alerts about its own problems. Use all three: the metrics and the rules tell you from outside, and the Internal alerts
reach you through Muster itself.

## Metrics

Muster serves `/metrics` on the **internal listener**, port 8082 by default (`MUSTER_LISTEN_INTERNAL`), next to
`/health/live` and `/health/ready`. It never pushes metrics. Do not expose that listener outside the cluster.

With the Prometheus Operator, set `serviceMonitor.enabled: true`. The chart then creates a `ServiceMonitor` for the
internal Service, with `serviceMonitor.interval` (default 30 seconds) and `serviceMonitor.scrapeTimeout` (default 10
seconds), and extra labels from `serviceMonitor.labels` for the selector of your Prometheus. Without the operator, scrape
the internal Service yourself, or the pods on port 8082.

Every metric is in the [metrics reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/metrics.md). Entities appear by their immutable id; their names are
in the `*_info` metrics, which the dashboard joins. No metric carries an alert label, a user or an Alert Group number.

## Alert rules

The chart renders one group of rules, named `muster`, when you enable one of:

`alerting.prometheusRule.enabled`
:   renders: a `PrometheusRule` · needs: the Prometheus Operator CRDs

`alerting.vmRule.enabled`
:   renders: a `VMRule` · needs: the VictoriaMetrics Operator CRDs

Both take extra labels (`alerting.prometheusRule.labels`, `alerting.vmRule.labels`) for the rule selector of your
operator. Each rule has a `description` and a `runbook_url` that points to its [runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/index.md), built from
`alerting.runbookBaseURL` and the version of Muster the chart deploys.

What you can tune:

- `alerting.jobSelector` is the label matcher that selects Muster's series in every rule. By default it is
  `job="muster"`, the job the `ServiceMonitor` gives. Change it when your scrape job has another name.
- `alerting.rules.<Name>.enabled` switches one rule off, and `.for` sets how long its condition holds before it fires.
- Some rules have thresholds: `window` (the range of the `rate` or `increase`), `seconds` (`MusterDeliverySlow`: p95
  delivery latency; `MusterClockSkew`: the skew), `size` (`MusterDeliveryQueueGrowing`), `backlog` and `delaySeconds`
  (`MusterIngestBacklog`), `unauthorized` (`MusterIngestRejected`) and `failures` (`MusterLoginFailures`).

The defaults are in the [chart values reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/chart-values.md), and the expression of each rule is on
its [runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/index.md) page. The rules are covered by unit tests in CI.

The five rules with severity `critical` are `MusterDown`, `MusterNoLeader`, `MusterDeliveryFailing`,
`MusterDestinationBroken` and `MusterHeartbeatLost`. The others are `warning`.

### Send the critical rules around Muster

!!! warning "Do not route the critical rules through Muster"
    A rule such as `MusterDown` or `MusterDeliveryFailing` fires when Muster cannot do its job. If Alertmanager sends
    it to Muster, the alert goes exactly where it cannot be delivered. Use an Alertmanager route that **bypasses** Muster
    for them, to a receiver you trust to work when Muster does not.

The chart rules carry the labels `alertname` (starting with `Muster`) and `severity: critical` or `warning`, plus the
labels Prometheus adds from the series. Match on both, and put the bypass route **first**, above the route that sends
everything to Muster, with `continue` false (the default) so that the alert stops there. Here it is added to the
configuration of [Connect Alertmanager](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/alertmanager.md), whose receivers `muster-prod-eu`, `oncall`
and `default` stay as they are:

```yaml
route:
  receiver: default
  routes:
    - receiver: platform-direct          # not Muster
      matchers: ['alertname=~"Muster.+"', 'severity="critical"']
    - receiver: muster-prod-eu
      continue: true
      repeat_interval: 10m
    - receiver: oncall
      matchers: ['severity="critical"']
    - receiver: default

receivers:
  # ... muster-prod-eu, oncall and default
  - name: platform-direct
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://chat.example.org/hooks/<id>          # a chat or a pager of your own
        send_resolved: true
```

The matchers use `alertname=~"Muster.+"` for the rules of this chart; `severity="critical"` limits the bypass to the ones
that need it, so the warnings still reach Muster, and every other alert still reaches Muster and your own receivers.
Point the receiver `platform-direct` at a path that does not depend on Muster.

The Internal alerts of Muster itself do not go through Alertmanager, so this route does not see them.

## Dashboard

The chart ships one dashboard, "Muster", with the fixed uid `muster`, a data source variable, and the variables
`namespace`/`job`, `integration`, `route` and `destination`. It has four rows: Overview, Ingestion, Delivery and
Platform. You enable it in either or both ways, each behind its own flag:

`dashboard.configMap.enabled`
:   renders: a `ConfigMap` with the dashboard JSON

    For the Grafana sidecar; `dashboard.configMap.labels` defaults to `grafana_dashboard: "1"`.

`dashboard.grafanaDashboard.enabled`
:   renders: a `GrafanaDashboard` of the Grafana Operator

    References that ConfigMap, so it needs `dashboard.configMap.enabled` too; `instanceSelector`, `folder` and
    `allowCrossNamespaceImport` are values.

## Internal alerts

Muster raises its own problems as **Internal alerts**: `MusterSnapshotTruncated`, `MusterHeartbeatLost`,
`MusterDestinationBroken`, `MusterTemplateError` and `MusterOIDCSecretExpiring`. They are Alerts of the built-in
"Muster" Integration, which has no tokens and cannot be changed. They go through Routes like any Alert, and they reach
nobody until a Route sends them to a Destination. The [Internal alerts reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/internal-alerts.md) lists
them with their labels.

Give them a Route:

1. Open **Routes**. At the top of the list, Muster suggests *Send Muster's own alerts to a Destination* when no Route
   other than the Default route matches them.
2. Choose a Destination, and press *Create the route*. The Route matches `alertname=~"Muster.*"`.

Use a Destination that does not depend on what the alert reports: not the one that is Broken. A second messenger, or an
[outgoing webhook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/outgoing-webhooks/events.md) to a chat of your own, serves well. When a Route for
`MusterHeartbeatLost` exists, the Internal alerts Route goes directly below it. Every Internal alert has a
[runbook](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/runbooks/index.md), and `MUSTER_RUNBOOK_BASE_URL` (set by the chart from `alerting.runbookBaseURL`) is the base
of its link.

Two Internal alerts have a chart rule with the same name, `MusterHeartbeatLost` and `MusterDestinationBroken`. The rule is
the backup for when Muster cannot deliver; the Internal alert carries the labels of what it is about: the Integration,
with its Static labels, for `MusterHeartbeatLost`, and the Destination for `MusterDestinationBroken`.

## Watching that Muster is alive

Metrics and rules need Prometheus. To notice that Muster, its cluster or its network is down altogether, configure the
[outgoing heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/outgoing-heartbeat.md): an external service alerts you when the calls stop.

The **System status** page (**Organization → System status**, Admins only) shows the same from the inside: the Leader and
every live replica with the key ids it holds, recovery after downtime, delivery queues, Broken Destinations, Integrations
that need attention, template errors, Storms and the outgoing heartbeat.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/outgoing-heartbeat.md -->
# Outgoing heartbeat

The metrics and the Internal alerts tell you about a Muster that runs. They cannot tell you that Muster, its node, its
cluster or its network is gone: a dead service raises nothing. For that, Muster calls a URL of your choice at a regular
interval, and a service outside Muster alerts you when the calls stop. This is a **dead man's switch**, and the call is
the **outgoing heartbeat**. It is the opposite direction of a [Heartbeat](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/integrations/heartbeat.md), which watches the
path *to* Muster.

## Pick a service

Any service that expects a regular HTTP request and alerts when it misses, and that sits outside the cluster Muster runs
in, will do:

- **Uptime Kuma**: a monitor of the type *Push*; it gives a URL and alerts when no call arrives within the interval.
- Any dead man's switch service that accepts an HTTP `GET` and alerts when the calls stop.

Set its expected period a little above Muster's interval of 1 minute, such as 2 or 3 minutes, so that a single slow call
does not alert. Send its alert somewhere that does not depend on Muster.

## Set it up

Open **Organization → Outgoing heartbeat**, as an Admin.

1. Enter the **Heartbeat URL** of the service.
2. If Muster must reach it through a proxy, fill the proxy form; it is the same form as everywhere, see
   [Proxies](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/proxies.md).
3. Save.

The URL is a **Secret**: such URLs carry a token. Muster encrypts it with the Keyring, never shows it again, and removes
it from every log line and error. The page shows whether it is set, and the Organization settings have no way to read it
back. To change it, enter the whole new URL.

Without a URL nothing is sent, and **System status** suggests setting one up: "Set up an outgoing heartbeat so that a
stopped Muster is noticed."

## What Muster sends

Interval
:   1 minute (`outgoing_heartbeat.interval`)

Method
:   `GET` (`outgoing_heartbeat.method`)

Timeout
:   10 seconds for one request (`outgoing_heartbeat.timeout`)

Retry
:   None: a failure is counted and logged, and the next tick is the retry.

Only the **Leader** sends it, so it stops when no replica leads, and it stops when Muster is down. Both are what you want
a dead man's switch to see. See [High availability](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/high-availability.md#the-leader). The call goes through the
[outbound address policy](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/proxies.md#what-the-outbound-address-policy-checks) like every other outbound
request, so a service on a private network needs an allowed entry under **Organization → Outbound addresses** when the
policy is strict.

## What the System status page shows

**Organization → System status** has a section *Outgoing heartbeat* with the last result:

- *Last sent {time}: OK*
- *Last sent {time}: {reason}*, where the reason is, for example, that the host name does not resolve, that no answer came
  in time, that the TLS handshake failed or that the URL refused the request
- *Not sent yet*, right after a start or a change

The settings page shows the same as *Last result: OK, sent {time}*, *Last result: not sent yet* and *Last result: nothing
is sent without a URL*. Check it after you save: it proves that Muster reaches the service.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/cli.md -->
# The command line

The `muster` binary is the server and its command line. Without a command it runs the server. The commands are for
emergencies, for setup and for diagnosis; everything else is in the web UI and the API. `muster help` lists them; its
output, abridged:

```text
Usage: muster [command]

Commands:
  migrate   Apply the database migrations under the migration lock
  doctor    Check the database, its connections, the master keys and the clock; only reads
  admin     Emergency access with --actor <name> <login>: admin reset-password sets a password read from standard
            input, admin reset-totp removes a lost second factor
  ingest    ingest replay --since <duration> [--integration <name>] --actor <name> reprocesses Stored Snapshots
  secrets   secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor <name> activates a master key that every live replica holds
  bridge    bridge check <url> --token-file <file> --channel <id> runs the Bridge protocol against a bridge, without a
            database; muster bridge help lists its flags
  dev       Development mode: fake servers and development defaults
  version   Print the version and commit
  help      Show this help
```

Every command exits 0 on success, 1 on a failure and 2 on a usage error, such as a missing flag.

## Environment

The commands that use the database read the same `MUSTER_*` variables as the server. Run them in the environment of the
server, not in a bare shell:

```sh
kubectl -n muster exec deploy/muster -- muster doctor
docker compose exec muster muster doctor
```

The image has no shell, so run the binary directly. A command that reads a password from standard input needs
`kubectl exec -i` or `docker compose exec -T`.

`doctor`, `migrate`, `secrets rotate-key`
:   Need the database settings, `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL` and the master keys (`MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS` or
    `MUSTER_SECRET_KEYS_FILE`).

`admin`, `ingest replay`
:   Need the database settings and `MUSTER_PUBLIC_URL`; they do not open the Keyring.

`bridge check`, `version`
:   Need nothing.

The [environment reference](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/reference/environment.md) lists the variables, and [the database](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/install/database.md)
the ways to set the connection.

## `--actor`

The commands that **change data** require `--actor <name>`: `admin reset-password`, `admin reset-totp`, `ingest replay`
and `secrets rotate-key`. The name says who runs the command. Muster writes it, with the Transport `cli`, to the Audit
log, so that a change made from a terminal has a person next to it like a change made in the web UI. Without `--actor` the
command exits 2 before it connects, and nothing changes. `migrate` and `doctor` take no `--actor`.

## `muster doctor`

```text
muster doctor
```

Checks and **only reads**. Each check prints one line, `OK`, `WARN` or `FAIL`, then its name and detail. The command
exits 1 when a check fails. A warning does not fail it.

`database`
:   Looks at: the main connection works.

`postgresql_version`
:   Looks at: PostgreSQL 14 or newer.

`session_connection`
:   Looks at: the session connection supports advisory locks and `LISTEN`, and the mode of each pooler.

`tls_main`, `tls_session`
:   Looks at: whether each connection is encrypted; `WARN`, not `FAIL`, when it is not.

`key_canary`
:   Looks at: the master keys can decrypt the canary, so they belong to this database.

`keyring`
:   Looks at: the active key is held, and which other keys are still needed, removable or not active yet.

`clock_skew`
:   Looks at: the replica's clock against the database clock, `WARN` above 2 seconds.

`connection <name>`, `destination <name>`
:   Looks at: the check of every Connection and every Destination that has one.

Run it after an install, after a [restore](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/backup-and-restore.md), after an [upgrade](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md), and when you suspect
the database, a pooler or the keys.

## `muster migrate`

```text
muster migrate
```

Applies the migrations under a session advisory lock and logs the versions it applied. It refuses to run on a schema
newer than the binary knows and names both versions. The Helm chart runs it in an init container. See
[Upgrades](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/upgrades.md#migrations).

## `muster admin`

```text
muster admin reset-password --actor <name> <login>
muster admin reset-totp --actor <name> <login>
```

Emergency access when no Admin can sign in. Flags come before the login.

- `reset-password` reads the new password from standard input: without echo after a prompt on a terminal, otherwise the
  first line. It sets it on the User with that login and ends the User's sessions. On a User who signs in through
  OpenID Connect, it also removes the OIDC identity, so the User signs in with the password from then on.
- `reset-totp` removes the TOTP and the recovery codes of the User, for a lost second factor, and ends their sessions.
  Under a TOTP policy that covers the User, they enrol again at the next sign-in. See [TOTP](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/sign-in/totp.md).

```sh
printf '%s\n' "$NEW_PASSWORD" | kubectl -n muster exec -i deploy/muster -- \
  muster admin reset-password --actor alice admin@example.org
```

## `muster ingest replay`

```text
muster ingest replay --since <duration> [--integration <name>] --actor <name>
```

Reprocesses Stored Snapshots, for example after a bug in processing was fixed.

- `--since` is the period back from now, such as `1h` or `90m`. A period longer than the retention of Stored Snapshots
  is cut to it.
- `--integration` limits the replay to the Integration with that name.

The command sets the Stored Snapshots of the period back to pending in one transaction and records `ingest.replayed` in
the Audit log; the running replicas process them again in arrival order. Processing is idempotent per Alert, so Snapshots
that were processed change nothing, while one that failed is processed with the current code. The command prints how many
Stored Snapshots it replayed.

## `muster secrets rotate-key`

```text
muster secrets rotate-key --activate <id> --actor <name>
```

Activates a master key, re-encrypts the Secrets and the key canary, and makes the Leader re-sign the buttons of open Root
messages. It refuses while a live replica does not hold the key. `--activate` is the key id that **Organization →
Keyring** shows. The two steps around it, and what to do afterwards, are in [Key rotation](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/key-rotation.md).

## `muster bridge check`

```text
muster bridge check <url> --token-file <file> --channel <id> [flags]
```

Runs the Bridge protocol against a bridge, step by step, and prints one line per step: `PASS`, `FAIL` with the reason, or
`SKIP`. It needs no database, master key or configuration, writes nothing, and never changes the bridge's configuration.
It exits 0 when no step failed, 1 when one did, and 2 on a usage error.

Flags: `--token-file` and `--channel` are required; `--forbidden-channel`, `--handle`, `--push-listen`, `--push-url`,
`--push-secret-file` and `--no-interactive` are optional. Their meaning, the steps and a worked example are in [Write a
bridge](https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/messengers/write-a-bridge.md#muster-bridge-check).

## `muster version`

```text
muster version
```

Prints the version and the commit, in the form `muster <version> (commit <sha>)`. The metric `muster_build_info` carries the
same two labels.

## `muster dev`

`muster dev` runs Muster with fake messenger servers and a published development master key. It is for working on Muster; do
not use it for an installation.

<!-- Source: https://muster-io.github.io/muster/latest/operations/request-log.md -->
# Request log

The **Request log** keeps the recent HTTP requests Muster sent to a messenger, a bridge or an outgoing webhook, and
those that reached a Connection's addresses, each with its answer and with secrets masked. It shows what Muster sent
and what came back when a Root message looks wrong, a check fails or a button press does nothing, without a packet
capture. It is neither the Audit log, which says who changed what, nor the Delivery events, which say what happened to
an Alert Group's delivery: the Request log keeps the requests themselves, for a short time.

## What is recorded

Each attempt of a request is a record of its own.

**Requests Muster sends** for a Connection or an outgoing webhook Destination: Root messages, their edits, Thread
replies, final edits, Storm summaries and deletions; test messages, and the button press a Mattermost test makes through
the bot (a Slack test makes none, because a bot cannot press its own button); answers to people, such as ephemeral
messages and callback answers; the requests of Account links, such as finding a person and sending a direct message;
channel lists, bridge info and webhook registration; event polling (Telegram `getUpdates`, Bridge `pollEvents`), and the
request that opens a Slack Socket Mode connection; and the requests of checks and tests — the Connection check, the
check before saving, also of a Connection that does not exist yet, the Destination check, the test message and the probe
of a Broken Destination.

**Requests that reach Muster** on the ingest listener, each with the answer Muster gave, refused ones included — a bad
signature, a wrong secret token, a Connection in the other event delivery mode:

`press`
`/api/v1/callbacks/mattermost/{connection_id}`
:   A button press in Mattermost.

`update`
`/api/v1/callbacks/telegram/{connection_id}`
:   A Telegram update in the webhook mode.

`push`
`/api/v1/callbacks/bridge/{connection_id}`
:   An event a bridge pushes.

`interactive`
`/api/v1/callbacks/slack/{connection_id}`
:   A button press in Slack, in the HTTP event mode. In Socket Mode there is no request to Muster: each envelope that
    carries an envelope id is recorded as received under its own type, with the socket's host as its URL, the
    envelope as its request and Muster's confirmation as its answer, without a status; the app subscribes to no events,
    so only `interactive` envelopes arrive. Slack's `hello`, `disconnect` and keep-alive frames are not recorded.

A record holds:

- the time, and the direction: **Sent** (→) or **Received** (←);
- the operation as its protocol names it: the method of the Telegram Bot API (`sendMessage`, `editMessageText`,
  `getUpdates`), the operation of Mattermost's REST API in lower camel case (`createPost`, `patchPost`, `getPing`), the
  operation of the Bridge protocol (`getInfo`, `postMessage`, `pollEvents`), the method of Slack's Web API as Slack
  names it (`chat.postMessage`, `chat.update`, `apps.connections.open`), `response_url` for an answer sent to a press's
  `response_url`, `event` or the request of a template (`create`, `update`, `open_thread`, `reply_in_thread`) for an
  outgoing webhook, and `press`, `update`, `push` or `interactive` for requests that reached Muster;
- the method, the URL, the request headers and body, and the answer's status, headers and body — none for a request
  that got no answer;
- the latency in milliseconds, the path — direct or through the proxy — and the attempt;
- for a request that failed, its error class, what failed — the codes of the checks, such as a DNS lookup that failed
  or no answer in time — and the error text;
